articles.title: Disgruntled troops leak PHOTOS of extensive damage to US bases from Iranian strikes
articles.body:
Disgruntled troops leak PHOTOS of extensive damage to US bases from Iranian strikes
US troops have leaked new images to CBS News capturing widespread destruction at American military bases across the Middle East from Iran’s missile and drone attacks.
The servicemen who provided the photos chose to stay anonymous because of harsh media restrictions in the US military, the outlet said in an article on Tuesday.
“This is major damage to our bases that hasn’t been communicated to the American public,” one of the soldiers stationed in the region said.
The service member complained about insufficient air defenses at the US facilities, saying “we’re standing there with our eyes closed getting punched in the face.”
The Iranian munitions that are getting through are “not ‘squirters’” as US Secretary of War Pete Hegseth called them after six American troops were killed in a strike on a US military tactical operations center at the Port of Shuaiba in Kuwait in early March, the soldier stressed. “We’re not defending these bases. We’re just watching them get destroyed.”
🚨🇺🇸 🇮🇷 BREAKING: Troops leaked photos of their wrecked bases to CBS, saying they're "standing there with our eyes closed getting punched in the face"
Active service members sent the images anonymously. 
One soldier's words: "We're not defending these bases. We're just watching… pic.twitter.com/zvxEyxB8wm
CBS News said that the photos it had received showed a $300 million US E-3 Sentry radar plane destroyed by a direct hit at Prince Sultan Air Force Base in Saudi Arabia as well as damaged buildings and burnt-out vehicles at Camp Buehring and Camp Arifjan in Kuwait.
Earlier this week, the US War Department’s inspector general issued a report, saying that the American forces have suffered $3.7 billion in equipment losses, including almost 60 aircraft, during the war against Iran, which started in late February with a US-Israeli attack on the Islamic Republic. 
American bases in Kuwait, Bahrain, Qatar, UAE, Saudi Arabia, Iraq, Oman and Jordan were hit, with hundreds of buildings and structures being damaged or destroyed, according to the inspector.
Last week, the acting secretary of the US Navy, Hung Cao, told the Epoch Times that Iran “blew the hell out of Bahrain,” referring to the attacks on the American military facilities in the Gulf country.
Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi responded to the acknowledgment in a post on X, saying that “our powerful Armed Forces did indeed ‘blow the hell out of the 5th Fleet HQ in Bahrain,’ as well as other bases supporting US aggression.”
In early September, Iranian Parliament speaker and top negotiator Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf warned that further aggressive actions by the US will be met with “faster, heavier and more painful” retaliation by Tehran.
“The Americans have surely understood that the era of proportionate responses has come to an end and our recent strikes against aggressor bases were only a start,” Ghalibaf said.

articles.title: Von der Leyen pitches European Security Council in response to Trump and Putin
articles.body:
European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen on Wednesday said she would propose a new security forum for EU and like-minded leaders in response to escalating Russian attacks and fraying transatlantic relations.
It's part of a broader rethink of security policy that includes a more robust response to hybrid attacks attributed to Russia and a greater effort to build up Europe's own defense capabilities — although in conjunction with NATO.
“For a long time, we have discussed a leaders' format focused on the security of our continent with partners like Ukraine, the U.K., Norway, Canada and others involved,” she said in her annual State of the European Union address.
Advertisement
“This is even more urgent now, given the nature and scale of the risks at play — this is why we will set out our ideas to make a European Security Council a reality,” she said. "The urgency is clear."
The proposal underscores growing fears that Europe is struggling to deal with rapidly proliferating airspace violations, cyberattacks and sabotage attempts amid tensions linked to the Kremlin's full-scale invasion of Ukraine, with NATO wary of escalating its response amid fears of setting off a war with Russia.
The transatlantic alliance has also been strained by growing tensions between U.S. President Donald Trump and European allies and Canada. Trump threatened to annex Greenland earlier this year, is recalibrating U.S. forces in Europe and has threatened Canadian sovereignty, fueling doubts over Washington’s commitment to the transatlantic alliance.
“This is a Europe that stands up for each other,” von der Leyen said, “like when we stood up for Greenland when threatened.”
Various versions of a European Security Council have been floated since the 1980s but none have gained traction. The idea resurfaced after an EU split over the 2003 Iraq war and was given fresh impetus in 2017 by former EU executive chief Jean-Claude Juncker and French President Emmanuel Macron, but failed because of U.K. reluctance.
Green MEP Sergey Lagodinsky resuscitated a formal proposal for a UN-style security council this year, arguing for an intergovernmental treaty that would bring together Germany, France, Italy, Spain, Poland and the U.K. alongside two rotating seats for smaller countries to speed decision-making in crises.
Advertisement
EU capitals have generally been skeptical of handing over their jealously guarded powers on defense to new institutions. The pitch also risks a clash with NATO, which has repeatedly warned Brussels against duplicating the alliance's security mission.
The Commission chief also said she would propose an EU emergency security protocol modeled on NATO’s Article 4 urgent consultation procedure to respond to hybrid attacks that fall below the threshold of armed aggression but still threaten national security.
“Europe needs its own counter-hybrid playbook,” she said. “When triggered by one member state, all member states would convene to coordinate a European response — to deter further escalation and to mitigate the impact.”
To bolster Europe’s efforts to take charge of its own defense, von der Leyen also floated a new scheme for building European strategic military capabilities such as air-to-air refueling and air and missile defense — areas where the continent still relies heavily on U.S. technology.
“I can announce a new European Instrument for strategic enablers — fully aligned with NATO,” she said. “These systems are essential, and we need more of them. Only together does Europe have the scale to deliver them.”
Manfred Weber, who leads the center-right European People’s Party group in the European Parliament, echoed that call and warned of the danger posed by Russian leader Vladimir Putin.
Advertisement
“The threat is clear — Putin won’t stop,” he said, speaking after von der Leyen's address. “Our answer is unity … joint command structures, European drones, European satellites so closely connected that no one can ever undo this cooperation.”
Weber said such joint action should reduce the fragmentation of European defense efforts, which leads to waste and duplication among member countries. The goal is not to create "27 bonsai armies," he said.

articles.title: A confession that shook the United States
articles.body:
A confession that shook the United States
Kayhan, in a note, addressed the first official Pentagon report acknowledging the scale of damage the United States suffered in the war against Iran. The US has incurred tens of billions of dollars in losses and has lost hundreds of military buildings and installations.
Trump launched the war with very specific goals like overthrowing the Islamic Republic, destroying Iran’s nuclear, missile, and drone capabilities, etc. But none of these objectives were achieved, and new problems emerged: Iran closed the Strait of Hormuz, the global economy entered crisis, inflation rose, and American farmers suffered losses. As the war dragged on and Iran launched extensive, heavy attacks on at least 20 US bases across eight regional countries, it became clear that many of these bases had suffered billions of dollars in damage and were no longer usable. The revelation triggered a political earthquake in the United States, prompting Trump and Pete Hegseth to deny the report quickly.
Resalat: Sending false signals of calm is dangerous
Resalat, in an analysis, warned about the most dangerous strategic trap at the current moment: sending “false signals of calm” to global markets. Iran’s diplomatic and media apparatus must be extremely vigilant so that news about the Oman talks is not framed by Western media as a sign that the reopening of the Strait of Hormuz is imminent. The reasons for this caution are: neutralizing Iran’s greatest leverage, buying time for war‑planners in the White House, and preventing public opinion from becoming conditioned. Iran must state clearly that the Oman understanding is a post‑war document, and until the White House ends its warmongering and accepts Tehran’s conditions, the energy and global transport crisis gripping the West will not end. The Muscat agreement should be presented to the world as proof of Iran’s responsibility and sovereign rights.
Sobh-e-No: The Salalah meeting had already been decided on the battlefield and in diplomacy
Sobh-e-No, in an article, assessed the reasons behind the cancellation of the Salalah meeting in Oman. The purpose of the meeting was to unveil a new plan for regulating traffic in the Strait of Hormuz and organizing maritime movement in this strategic waterway. But the meeting was postponed indefinitely. A closer look at recent developments shows that the cancellation was a direct result of a fundamental shift in the regional balance of power: significant advances by Ansarallah, the resistance front’s control over two strategic straits (Bab al‑Mandab and Hormuz), and explosions along Saudi Arabia’s east‑west pipeline and disruptions in its oil exports. The cancellation benefited Tehran, reinforcing the new strategic reality. Iran now watches calmly as developments unfold in ways that increase its strategic weight in the Persian Gulf. In essence, the Salalah meeting encountered a reality that had already been shaped on the battlefield and in diplomacy, long before any agreement could be drafted on paper.
Etemad: Iran must strengthen its initiatives
Etemad, in an interview with Amir Asgar, senior researcher and strategic security analyst, discussed Iran’s policy and initiative in the current situation. According to Asgar, alongside diplomatic engagement with Persian Gulf states, Iran must intensify its influence in Yemen and alternative energy routes—both militarily and diplomatically. Iran must be the actor that determines what happens in the Strait of Hormuz. If Iran loses initiative and the control of escalation—whether diplomatic or military—falls into American hands, Iran will face serious challenges. This is not an issue that can be simplified under the assumption that it can be resolved solely through negotiations, because it directly concerns national security. The postponement of the meeting could allow Iran to take control of escalation management through other channels, a matter that is vital for the country.
Shargh: Tehran and Baghdad work to contain the fallout of ongoing regional developments
Shargh, in an analysis, examined the gradual reopening of the Iran–Iraq border, describing it as a sign of Tehran and Baghdad’s efforts to manage the consequences of ongoing regional developments on bilateral relations. These developments, if they continue, could affect the economic, security, and commercial ties between the two countries. The attack on infrastructure that serves as Saudi Arabia’s alternative route to the Strait of Hormuz, combined with conflicting claims about the origin of the attack and Baghdad’s security responses, shows how any incident in the region’s tense environment can quickly escalate from a limited security event into an issue with political, economic, and regional dimensions. In such circumstances, Iraq’s investigation into the origin of the attack and related actors becomes even more important. What is clear for now is the effort by Tehran and Baghdad to maintain coordination and prevent escalation, while Saudi Arabia simultaneously works to protect one of its most important oil transit routes.

articles.title: Russian army loses snother 1,530 troops, four air defense systems in war against Ukraine
articles.body:
Russian army loses another 1,530 troops, four air defense systems in war against Ukraine
The General Staff of the Armed Forces of Ukraine stated this on Facebook, Ukrinform reports.
In addition, the Russian army has lost 12,345 tanks (+0), 25,339 armored combat vehicles (+5), 49,820 artillery systems (+27), 2,132 multiple rocket launchers (+1), 1,642 air defense systems (+4), 442 aircraft (+0), 356 helicopters (+0), 2,630 ground robotic systems (+4), 519,069 operational-tactical UAVs (+789), 5,111 cruise missiles (+0), 35 ships/boats (+0), 2 submarines (+0), 149,557 vehicles and fuel trucks (+374), and 4,692 units of special equipment (+2).
The figures are being assessed.
As Ukrinform reported, Commander of the Third Army Corps, Brigadier General Andrii Biletskyi, confirmed reports of a Ukrainian army offensive in the northern part of Donetsk region. The Defense Forces have so far cleared 75 square kilometers and liberated 10 square kilometers.

articles.title: Ukraine’s Third Army Corps command reveals a months-old counteroffensive in northern Donetsk region. Its ultimate goal remains unknown.
articles.body:
Ukraine’s Third Army Corps command reveals a months-old counteroffensive in northern Donetsk region. Its ultimate goal remains unknown.
The Command of the Ukrainian Ground Forces’ Third Army Corps said its forces are conducting a counteroffensive in the northern Donetsk region. The corps commander, Brigadier General Andrii Biletskyi, described the operation in a special video address. Pro-war Russian bloggers had previously reported a Ukrainian offensive near the city of Lyman (1, 2, 3).
The Ukrainian Armed Forces have named the operation “Vivaldi.” Biletskyi said that during the offensive, the Third Corps had “cleared out infiltrating forces” in several communities along the Lyman axis — Novoselivka, Oleksandrivka, Yarova, and the area around Korovyi Yar — and liberated Serednie. In total, Ukrainian forces cleared 75 square kilometers and liberated another 10 square kilometers from Russian troops. They also allegedly “dealt a devastating blow to the combat capabilities of Russia’s 20th and 25th armies.” This information has not been independently verified.
Biletskyi said that at this stage of the operation, Russian forces have lost about 1,500 soldiers — though he did not specify whether the figure referred only to troops killed, captured, missing, or otherwise permanently lost — as well as more than 12,000 drones and hundreds of armored vehicles, artillery systems, and other vehicles. He also said Ukrainian drones had cut off the enemy’s supply routes.
“There is a lot of information in open sources right now saying that the ultimate goal of our offensive is to reach the banks of the Zherebets River. But our operation is called ‘Vivaldi.’ And as everyone knows, Vivaldi has four seasons. This is only the first,” Biletskyi said.
Biletskyi urged people to continue maintaining “operational secrecy” and promised updates on the operation from official sources. The Ukrainian operation in the Donetsk region has been underway for about four months, but officials had not previously disclosed it. Its ultimate goal remains unknown.
Lyman is a strategically important city roughly 100 kilometers north of Russian-occupied Donetsk. Russian forces captured it in May 2022, but Ukraine regained control of the city in October of that year. In early summer 2026, Russian forces again tried to storm Lyman but failed.
Meduza’s Razbor team will soon examine what is happening in this sector of the front in its next battlefield update.
The war in photos: Kramatorsk
A Russian airstrike destroyed a private home in Kramatorsk, a city 40 kilometers from Lyman. Olena and Yana lived there. They survived only because they were at a city market when the strike occurred. Nothing remains of the house but ruins. The photos were taken on September 16, 2026.
At Meduza, we are committed to transparency about our use of artificial intelligence in the newsroom. The story you’re reading was written by one of our living, breathing journalists and translated from Russian using an AI model configured to follow our strict editorial standards. This translation process is the result of extensive testing and refinements to ensure our English-language coverage is timely and accurate. A Meduza editor reviews every draft before publication.
If you find any errors in this translation, please contact us at [email protected].

articles.title: Houthis deny report they planted mines in Bab al-Mandeb
articles.body:
Breadcrumb
Houthis deny Yemen military claim they laid mines in Bab al-Mandeb
An anonymous Yemeni military source has accused the Houthis of laying mines in the Bab al-Mandeb Strait, a week after the group captured the Red Sea coast from government forces, German news agency DPA reported on Tuesday.
The Iran-aligned group effectively took control of the strait last week after routing Saudi-backed forces, threatening renewed disruption through the vital maritime corridor.
The Houthis have also reportedly begun fortifying their positions in the mountains overlooking the strait in anticipation of a counter-offensive by pro-government forces.
Hussain Al-Bukhaiti, a pro-Houthi Sanaa-based journalist, told The New Arab that the report was “false news”.
“Why do we need to put mines in the Red Sea or in Bab al-Mandeb if we have anti-ship ballistic missiles? We can launch attacks against any ship we choose,” he said.
Since taking control of the area, the Houthis have said they would uphold freedom of navigation through the strait but continue to impose a blockade on Saudi ships.
Arab and European countries have expressed alarm over the advance, which consolidates Houthi control over the strait and comes as the waterway has become increasingly important for Saudi oil shipments since the US-Israeli war on Iran shuttered the Strait of Hormuz.
Oil markets have been on edge over the past week as the Houthis' gains and a drone strike on Saudi Arabia's East-West pipeline have triggered fresh concerns about global supply.
The attack, which Saudi authorities said was launched from Iraq, has taken the pipeline offline, forcing the kingdom to rely exclusively on shipments through the Strait of Hormuz, assisted by the US military. Oil prices surged to their highest levels since May following the news.
The Houthis and the Yemeni government have engaged in fierce fighting since the collapse of the ceasefire in July.
The group has declared a blockade on Saudi ports and targeted Saudi ships in the Red Sea.
US-Houthi talks
US officials held talks with Houthi representatives in Oman over the weekend, a few days after their advance on the Red Sea coast, five sources familiar with the matter told Reuters.
The meeting was reportedly arranged by Oman and held at the US embassy in Muscat.
The Trump administration designated the Houthis as a terrorist organisation in March 2025 but later entered negotiations with them to end the two-month conflict.
Saudi Arabia's Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman has appealed to the US and UK to provide military support in its fight against the Houthis. The Trump administration reportedly told Riyadh it would not get directly involved.
Bin Salman travelled to Cairo on Tuesday to discuss the situation with Egyptian President Abdel Fattah al-Sisi.
A statement by Egypt's presidency said the two leaders called for freedom of navigation through the Red Sea to be maintained.
Drone over Mecca
The Saudi-led coalition on Wednesday accused the Houthis of targeting Mecca, triggering condemnations across the Muslim world.
A coalition spokesperson said its forces had allegedly intercepted a drone over the holy city.
Houthi armed forces spokesperson Yahya Saree denied the claims, calling them “fabrications and lies”.
“Our operations target its oil facilities and military bases, which are far removed from the sacred sites,” he said.
The Saudi coalition vowed retaliation, saying that “the security of the Two Holy Mosques and the pilgrims is a red line”.
The Organisation of Islamic Cooperation, a bloc of 57 Muslim countries, denounced the “heinous attacks... against the city of Mecca and the Madinah region”.
The Houthis also said on Wednesday that they had shot down a Saudi warplane.
“The Yemeni Armed Forces, with Allah's help and grace, succeeded in shooting down a Saudi F-15 fighter jet while it was carrying out hostile operations in support of its military buildup in the skies of Marib province,” Saree said in a statement.
Saudi warplanes have launched more than 450 airstrikes in Yemen this week, he said.

articles.title: British Army moves to restore long-range anti-tank strike
articles.body:
The British Army is moving to restore a beyond-line-of-sight anti-armour capability more than 30 years after Swingfire left service, with MBDA and Thales awarded contracts to explore a new weapon system, Defence Readiness and Industry Minister Luke Pollard has announced.
Speaking at DVD 2026, Pollard said the work would examine technologies for a weapon able to engage armoured targets beyond direct line of sight, improving the ability of British land forces to strike from greater distance while reducing their exposure on the battlefield.
He said: “And thirdly, I can also announce today that we have awarded contracts to MBDA and Thales to explore how we can develop the tech behind a new beyond-line-of-sight anti-armour weapon system, a capability that the British Army has not had since Swingfire, left service over 30 years ago, a capability that can drastically improve the ability of our land forces to strike and survive on the modern battlefield.”
Swingfire was a wire-guided anti-tank missile developed for the British Army and notable for its ability to turn sharply after launch, allowing the firing vehicle to remain concealed while the missile was guided onto a target from another position.
Its withdrawal left the Army without an equivalent long-range ground-launched anti-armour system able to engage targets beyond direct line of sight, with more recent anti-tank weapons generally centred on shorter-range engagements.
The new work with MBDA and Thales forms part of the Army’s wider Recce Strike concept, which is intended to combine surveillance, targeting, drones, armoured vehicles and longer-range weapons into a more connected force.
Pollard described the approach as being built around “better targeting, better battlefield surveillance and more lethal long range fire”, with the aim of improving both the speed and effectiveness of targeting.
The Government is committing more than £19 billion to land warfare capabilities over the next four years, alongside £11 billion for weapons and ammunition.
That includes £190 million for short-range ballistic missiles, £400 million for inexpensive one-way attack drones and weapons, and £220 million for Project Nyx, which is intended to develop armed autonomous aircraft capable of operating alongside Apache attack helicopters.
Another £370 million is being spent on Project Asgard, the digital command-and-control architecture supporting the Army’s Recce Strike model.
Pollard said: “That’s about improving the lethality and delivering against CGS’s 20:40:40 strategy, which has been baked into the Defence Investment Plan. Now, that will be collectively a higher resolution picture of the battlefield and increase the effectiveness and speed of our targeting.”
The new anti-armour work is also being tied directly to lessons from Ukraine, where long-range fires, drones and distributed targeting have changed how armoured forces are detected and engaged.
Pollard said: “Now, these are just three procurements that will not only demonstrate how we’re evolving operationally in response to the lessons from Ukraine, but they’re programmes that demonstrate how we have reformed our procurement processes in response to what we’ve learned from our friends in Ukraine.”
The MBDA and Thales contracts are therefore an early step towards restoring a capability absent from the Army for decades, while fitting into a wider effort to connect reconnaissance and long-range strike more closely across the land force.

articles.title: Lisa Nandy brands Musk’s X a ‘disgrace’ as she pledges crackdown on social media doxxing – UK politics live
articles.body:
Burnham rejects suggestion he's just 'traditional tax and spend socialist', saying he will take 'difficult decisons'
In his pooled TV clip, Andy Burnham firmly rejected suggestions that he is a traditional tax and spend socialist.
When Beth Rigby asked him to respond to Andy Haldane, the former Bank of England chief economist, who said in an interview last night that Burnham needed to persuade the financial markets he is not just “a traditional tax and spend socialist government with better TikTok videos” (see 10.58am), Burnham replied:
That doesn’t tell the story. We are not that.
Already I have taken difficult decisions in this job, in relation to re-prioritising government spending, putting digital ID on hold, for instance.
So it’s not the case that we aren’t going to take difficult decisions.
We will take difficult decisions to make sure the economy remains on track.
Schools in England to get almost £500m extra in bid to avoid strike by teachers over pay
Schools in England are set to receive additional funding to cover the costs of the teachers’ pay award, the UK’s largest teaching union has claimed. The Press Assocation reports:
The leader of the National Education Union (NEU), which has been preparing a formal ballot of its members on strike action, said the move signalled “a welcome return to reality” and a “message of hope” for school staff.
In July, the government accepted the recommendations of the School Teachers’ Review Body (STRB) for teachers to receive a 3.5% pay rise from this month, but the Department for Education (DfE) said schools would be expected to fund some of the pay award out of their existing budgets.
But in a letter to the NEU on Wednesday, education secretary Lucy Powell said schools can use savings in employers’ contributions to the local government pension scheme to help cover the costs of pay rises for school staff.
The letter, seen by the Press Association, said the 4.9 percentage point reduction in what employers are expected to contribute will deliver “significant savings” on the pay bill for support staff.
Powell said: “We can confirm this reduction in costs will not be clawed back and as such, we are confident that schools will be able to cover the costs of the teacher pay award, at a national level.”
In the letter to the NEU, she added: “Given the material change to the affordability position, I would ask that the NEU revisits its proposed ballot of members planned for October and moves away from strike action.”
On Wednesday, the NEU claimed it had secured “a fully funded pay increase” for all teachers throughout England, and called it a “significant step”.
The NEU has been preparing a formal ballot for strike action, which was due to begin on 3 October and close on 15 December.
The union’s national executive will now meet on 24 September to discuss its response to the letter.
Daniel Kebede, general secretary of the NEU, said: “Finally, we have a government that accepts the reality that any teacher pay award must be fully funded.
“Plugging the £460m black hole in school budgets signals a welcome return to reality, and a message of hope for the entire school community.
“Be in no doubt that the significant ground conceded by government is a consequence of NEU members’ willingness to take a stand.”
Burnham says UK's commitment to Nato 'unwavering' as he meets its secretary general, Mark Rutte
Andy Burnham assured Nato chief Mark Rutte that the UK’s commitment to the alliance remains despite the change in prime minister. As the Press Association reports, the Nato secretary general wished Mr Burnham “good luck” in the job as the two met face-to-face for the first time to discuss defence issues.
Burnham said:
There’s been a change of prime minister but never any change in the UK’s unwavering commitment to Nato and our Nato obligations … It’s critical for us always to show our firm commitment to Nato, and that’s what we will be doing today.
Rutte told him the UK was “one of the leading forces in Nato”.
The two met at RAL Space, a research facility in Didcot, Oxfordshire and Rutte praised the UK as a scientific and technological leader within the alliance.
TUC votes to back pro-Palestinian BDS movement and for full arms embargo against Israel
Aletha Adu
Aletha Adu is a Guardian political correspondent.
The TUC has voted to endorse the Boycott, Divestment, Sanctions (BDS) movement in a direct challenge to Ed Miliband’s bid to severely condemn Israel’s occupation of the West Bank as unlawful in its entirety.
Last week Miliband, the foreign secretary announced sweeping sanctions on trade with Israeli settlements which marked a huge shift in the UK’s position becoming the first UK foreign secretary to describe what is happening in the West Bank as ethnic cleansing.
But he now faces pressure from unions representing five million workers who have voted to pressure governments to uphold their legal obligations following the ICJ rulings of 2024 ... at a minimum by imposing a full arms embargo on Israel.
The motion proposed by the Artists’ Union also called for an escalation of “economic, academic, cultural and sports BDS campaigns”.
“BDS is an effective strategy to put pressure on Israel to end its ongoing genocide”, the motion added.
It marks a sharp rejection of Miliband’s actions, as he specifically condemned the BDS movement when announcing the sweeping sanctions as part of a passionate speech in the Commons last week. He said BDS targets the entire Israeli economy and not just occupied territories.
The motion from the Artists’ Union also called for “protection of artistic expression on Palestine”, and for artists, culture and education workers to not be forced to handle goods they believe breach international law if they don’t want to.
TUC delegates confirmed their support for workplace days of action for Palestine from 20 to 29 November.
There are a number of Labour MPs who do privately support the BDS movement, but still support Miliband for making an unprecedented move.
Commenting on the result, Peter Leary, deputy director of the Palestine Solidarity Campaign, said:
This historic vote, committing the TUC to support the Palestinian-led movement for boycott, divestment and sanctions, recognises that the limited steps announced by the government fall far short of meeting Britain’s legal obligations not to assist Israel’s ongoing genocide, apartheid, illegal occupation and other violations of international law. Trade unions and workers across Britain are right to call for continued political pressure and action in the workplace to end the complicity of companies, institutions and the government in Israel’s crimes against the Palestinian people.
In response to the call from Palestinian trade unions and the BDS movement, workers across Britain, alongside workers from around the world, will put this motion into practice on Thursday 26 November when they take part in the TUC-backed workplace day of action in solidarity with Palestine.
At least five Reform councillors joined Facebook group linked to far-right Patriot Platform
At least five Reform UK councillors have been members of a Facebook group linked to the far-right group involved in the blockades of Dover and Portsmouth by masked men, according to anti-fascist campaigners. Ben Quinn and Amelia Gentleman have the story.
DHSC announces local health partnerships as part of shifting focus from treatment to prevention
The Department of Health and Social Care has announced that it is going to pilot a new form of local, health partnership. They will focus on joined-up prevention.
The initiatives will involve NHS organisations, councils and community groups working together to tackle health inequalities. They will launched in: Bristol; Lewisham; north-east Lincolnshire; 19 boroughs of London; North Nottinghamshire; and York and Scarborough.
The projects will help more people receive joined-up support earlier, avoid unnecessary hospital admissions and remain independent for longer.
The six sites will develop and test new neighbourhood health models that bring together NHS services, councils, community organisations and local people to improve outcomes and tackle inequalities.
They will pave the way for the future so more areas can benefit from the innovative partnership model. The funding will help sites develop and test new neighbourhood health models, creating the foundations for larger-scale investment and wider adoption across the NHS in future.
The government has partnered with Social Finance, Macmillan Cancer Support and West Hertfordshire Teaching Hospitals NHS Trust. This will bring together expertise in cancer care, system transformation, innovative finance and neighbourhood health. Integrated Care Boards and local government partners across England were invited to apply.
The projects will be backed £1.5m in funding from the Office for the Impact Economy, a government body that works with “impact investors” – people wanting to invest private capital for a social good.
The government argues that these models could provide a model for the future because current health funding models don’t incentivise health providers to spend money on preventative measures that will stop people going to hospital.
Diana Johnson, the health minister, said:
The programme is a key part of our 10-year health plan, helping us shift from treating sickness to preventing it in the first place, and giving people the help they need in the heart of their own communities.
Burnham should appoint a deputy PM, says former cabinet secretary Simon Case, as he calls for written constitution
Andy Burnham should formally appoint a deputy PM, the former cabinet secretary Simon Case has said.
Case said he thought the appointment was necessary because in a country like Britain there should be absolutely no doubt about who might take over in the event of the PM being incapacitated.
He made his comment in evidence to the Lords constitutional affairs committee where he also said he had gradually come round to the idea that Britain needs a written constitution – in part because of the risk of informal constitutional conventions being ignored by rogue actors.
Case said he first became convinced of the need for the government to have a deputy PM when Boris Johnson became so ill with Covid in 2020 that his life was at risk. At the time Dominic Raab was the de facto deputy, as first secretary of state.
Raab was made deputy PM in 2021 and since then every PM before Burnham appointed a deputy.
Burnham does not have a deputy. But Louise Haigh is first secretary of state, and second to Burnham in the cabinet order of precedence.
At the committee hearing, John Cryer put it to Case that everyone assumed that, in the event of something happening to Burnham, Haigh would take over.
Case replied:
My assumption is the same as yours. This title, first secretary of state … is conveying the sense that this person fulfills that deputy role. But, as you said, these are assumptions that we’re making
We’re a $4 trillion economy, a nuclear power, a P5 nation [one of the five permanent members of the UN security council]. You and I shouldn’t be sitting here having to make assumptions about who’s in charge if the prime minister is unavoidable. I mean, come on.
Case said that over time his views on the need for written constitution had changed. He said that he did not think important process decisions should be left up to “the whim of a prime minister of the day”.
As an example of how some constitutional rules are unclear, Case confirmed reports that, when Johnson was facing a leadership challenge, some of his team thought he could avoid being forced out by his own MPs by calling a snap election. Case said:
When Boris Johnson’s cabinet ministers were resigning left, right and centre and his government was falling apart, some – well, I’ll leave them unnamed - uninformed individual around Boris Johnson decided to float the idea of whether it would be time to call a general election as a way of avoiding him being sort of brought down by his own party.
Case said he had to see off the idea by digging out a copy of the so-called Lascelles principles – a letter to the Times, sent anonymously by the king’s private secretary in 1950, that explains when it is appropriate for the monarch to refuse a request from a PM to call an election. The letter has no legal status, but is now taken as part of the unwritten constitution.
Explaining how his views had changed, Case said:
As time has gone on, I’m one of those people who’ve been on a rather long journey on this, becoming more and more convinced that we should be heading towards a more codified and written constitution.
But Case also said he was a “pragmatist”, and did not think this would happen for “a very, very long time”.
At the committee, Lord Strathclyde, the chair, suggested to Case that a cabinet secretary could stop a PM acting inappropriately by resigning, or threatening to resign.
In his reply, Case said:
I’m not entirely sure that the resignation of a cabinet secretary would have that impact. Perhaps in years gone by that might be true.
But cabinet secretaries these days are becoming a little bit like prime ministers and London buses - they come and go.
At Westminster it is normal for MPs who defect from one party to another to resist calls for a byelection, partly by arguing that they were personally elected.
But in the Senedd elections in May, MSs (members of the Senedd) were for the first time elected by the closed proportional list system, with each constituency electing six members.
Sarah Cooper-Lesadd, the lead candidate for Reform UK, Pen-y-Bont Bro Morgannwg (Bridgend and Vale of Glamorgan) was elected as a direct result of people voting for Reform UK. But she will now sit as a Plaid Cymru MS and vote for Plaid policies.
Under this election system, Cooper-Lesadd cannot resign and trigger a byelection. If she were to resign, her seat would be taken by the next person on the Reform UK list in that constituency.
In a post on social media, Joe Martin, a Reform UK MS, said her position was “completely untenable”. He went on:
No one, literally no one, voted for her in May’s election. The votes that put her in Parliament were for Reform UK. Specifically, they were to scrap the nation of sanctuary, prevent the breakup of the UK, and to deliver Reform’s manifesto.
This means she has no mandate to represent those people any longer. The people of Pen-y-bont Bro Morgannog wanted a voice in Reform. Instead, they’ve been used as a springboard for the political ambitions of Sarah Cooper-Lesadd. That simply isn’t right.
If you believe in Plaid Cymru, stand for Plaid Cymru. Don’t deceive your way through a selection process to stand where you think is most opportune to realise your own ambitions. A party with any sense would drop her like a stone at the next election.
In a separate post, Matthew MacKinnon, Reform UK’s director of external affairs, said Cooper-Lesadd should resign.
She was elected on a list system under a Reform banner with a clear intention to pursue her own agenda and not @RUKWales
She was not elected as an independent.
She has shamefully manipulated the party and the electorate.
She should resign.
Today James Evans, one of the Reform UK MSs, said he will not stand for leader. There is a vacancy after Dan Thomas resigned yesterday after being arrested and bailed on suspicion of assault and controlling or coercive behaviour.
According to a Spectator piece by James Heale, who is writing a book about Reform UK, Helen Jenner, the current deputy leader, is a favourite to replace Thomas. Heale says:
Jenner is Kipper royalty: a long-marcher whose husband is a good friend of Nigel Farage. Likeable and modest, she was working as a school teacher just weeks before being selected for the Senedd.
Pip more prone to abuse compared to equivalent disability benefits abroad due to design flaws, report says
The government is under pressure to cut the amount of money spent on disability benefits, particularly the personal independence payment, a non-means tested benefit that helps people with the costs they incur as a result of their disability.
In a report out today, Re:State, a centrist/right-leaning thinktank focusing on public sector reform, says the amount being spent on Pip is too high. It says other, equivalent benefits in prosperous democracies have much tighter rules and, as a result, work more effectively.
In particular, it highlights the fact that, while Pip claimants have to provide evidence of their disability, they do not have to provide evidence of the extra costs they are incurring as a result. “The requirement for evidence of extra costs is common in international models, but entirely absent from Britain’s model,” it says.
The report concludes:
Britain stands alone on a number of fundamental decisions. Pip has been designed to maximise administrative simplicity at the cost of accuracy, transparency, and perception of fairness. No other country relies solely on a functional assessment to determine extra-cost entitlement, without requiring evidence of the costs the benefit is intended to help meet. This creates a system which is vulnerable to gaming, and poorly equipped to distinguish between different levels of genuine need.
Additionally, Pip’s broad definition of extra costs means that its daily living component overlaps substantially with services that other countries address through social care and local provision. Elsewhere, clearer boundaries allow different parts of the state to perform different functions and reduce the risk of paying twice for the same need.
In incapacity benefits, versus the comparison countries, Britain appears to have a low bar for access; a less rigorous application and assessment process; and much weaker work incentives. Some of the comparator countries also make much greater use of employer responsibilities, intended to prevent people requiring incapacity benefits in the first place. It appears highly likely these design choices contribute to a greater proportion of Britain’s working-age population claiming incapacity benefits and a much greater proportion claiming incapacity benefits without any conditionality, as well as Britain’s comparably high disability employment gap.
The lesson from international experience is therefore not simply that Britain spends too much or that other countries have better systems. It is that design choices have consequences. How need is defined, where responsibility sits, what evidence is required, and what incentives are created all affect caseloads, expenditure, employment, and public confidence.
Pepper spray in young offender institutions used disproprotionately against black boys, prison charity says
Last year the Home Office announced that prison officers would be allowed to use Pava, a form of pepper spray, to incapacitate children at young offender institutions.
Today the Howard League for Penal Reform, which opposed the move, has released figures showing that Pava has been used disproportionately against black boys. In a news release, it says:
In April 2025, Shabana Mahmood, the then secretary of state for justice, gave the green light for Pava spray to be used in three prisons in England, holding boys as young as 15 – Feltham A, Werrington and Wetherby. The Howard League understands that deployment began in August for Werrington and Wetherby and in September for Feltham A.
Figures provided to the Howard League in response to a Freedom of Information Act request show that in the first few months of deployment, up to the end of March 2026, Pava spray was drawn and used against 33 children and young people in total – 19 in Feltham A and 14 in Werrington. In Wetherby, Pava spray was drawn on at least one occasion but not used.
Of the 33 children and young people who had Pava spray used against them, 18 were Black and six were white. Despite comprising only about 30% of the population in Feltham A and Werrington, Black children and young people were on the receiving end about 55% of the time.
Gemma Abbott, legal director at the Howard League, said:
Pava is a chemical irritant spray that can cause severe pain, and it is classified as a prohibited weapon under the Firearms Act 1968. It is shameful that prison staff have been given the power to use it against children.
Burnham says he will 'look at issues raised' in Piddington referendum, but insists small boat crossings 'signficantly down'
Andy Burnham was also asked about the Piddington anti-migrant camp independence vote in his pooled TV interview. Adopting the same tone as Lisa Nandy earlier (see 10am), he said he would “look at the issues being raised by the community and in the referendum”. But he said the government had a plan to get the number of small boat arrivals down and that it was working.
He said:
I understand the strength of feeling, and that’s something that is across the country. But the only thing to do is to get the number of crossings down, and they are significantly down.
Here is Ben Quinn’s story about the Piddington vote.
Burnham declines to commit to impose cap on amount individuals can donate to political parties
Andy Burnham has refused to commit to imposing a cap on the amount individuals can donate to political parties.
He has also declined to say whether he thinks the laws currently being passed by parliament, which will restrict the amount Britons can gave give to parties if they have recently move to the UK after living abroad, will result in Reform UK having to give back the £72m it has had from Ben Delo and Christopher Harborne, the two cryptocurrency billionaires.
Asked specifically if these donations would become impermissible, and if he would now back a cap on individual donations, Burnham replied:
The details of those donations are a matter for Reform, and they will have to account for the detail of how those donations have been made and whether they are permissible within the law. The government set out plans in the representation of the people bill to cap overseas donations. And that bill is going through parliament as we speak.
So it’s really important that we uphold the highest standards of trust, confidence, cleanliness in British politics. And that is incumbent on all politicians and all political parties.
Burnham said he was in favour of a cap on donations before he became PM. But many Labour-supporting union leaders do not back the idea, because they fear this could limit their ability to donate to the party, and Burnham has more recently backed away from the idea.
Burnham rejects suggestion he's just 'traditional tax and spend socialist', saying he will take 'difficult decisons'
In his pooled TV clip, Andy Burnham firmly rejected suggestions that he is a traditional tax and spend socialist.
When Beth Rigby asked him to respond to Andy Haldane, the former Bank of England chief economist, who said in an interview last night that Burnham needed to persuade the financial markets he is not just “a traditional tax and spend socialist government with better TikTok videos” (see 10.58am), Burnham replied:
That doesn’t tell the story. We are not that.
Already I have taken difficult decisions in this job, in relation to re-prioritising government spending, putting digital ID on hold, for instance.
So it’s not the case that we aren’t going to take difficult decisions.
We will take difficult decisions to make sure the economy remains on track.
Andy Burnham has said the budget will be “challenging”.
In his pooled TV interview, asked if the budget would be “difficult”, Burnham replied:
It’s going to be challenging because the picture around the world is challenging and particularly the situation in the Middle East. And we will look carefully at all of those things.
We won’t take risks with people’s living standards or with the economy as a whole. So we will take it all into account.
It’s why we wanted to do an earlier budget. We didn’t want to leave a long period of speculation. I think that’s been shown now to be the right decision.
It will mean taking whatever action we can to help people while also making sure we apply the highest degree of prudence to the running of the economy.
Talking about the state of the economy generally, he said he thought it was resilient.
If you look at the the detailed picture underlying today’s inflation figures, it shows resilience across the board, actually, in the British economy.
Burnham said the inflationary pressures were “driven by the situation in the Middle East”, which was a problem for countries around the world.
Burnham says his dad 'would want me back out there' as he returns to work after father's death
Andy Burnham has said that his father would have wanted him back at work.
In a pooled TV clip with Beth Rigby from Sky News, the PM spoke about the messages he had received since his father died on Monday.
He told Rigby:
It is hard, and it will be hard for a little while. But better to get back to the job.
But I also want to thank the leaders of the other parties, all of whom sent a message. It shows there is decency in British politics still, and that’s that’s what we need to see.
So it’s a thank you from us all, the whole family. But my dad would want me to be back out there … bringing some of the changes that he always pushed me to make.

articles.title: The Armored Sarcophagus Saving Ukrainian Soldiers
articles.body:
The Armored Sarcophagus Saving Ukrainian Soldiers
Unmanned ground vehicles are conducting once-impossible medical evacuations along Ukraine’s front lines.
Sign up for our newsletter about national security here.
The inside of an armored sarcophagus smells of gunpowder, gasoline, and gangrene. Remotely operated, unmanned ground vehicles, nicknamed MAULs, are revolutionizing casualty evacuations along the most dangerous sections of the Ukrainian front lines. They bristle with drone-jamming antennae and carry bulletproof black pods for carrying wounded soldiers to safety.
The MAUL goes in when other options have failed. After every rescue, it is cleaned and disinfected. Vitaly, call sign “Ash,” is a medical-evacuation coordinator with the 1st Separate Medical Battalion. (He asked to be identified only by his first name and call sign for security reasons.)
“You scrub and scrub,” he told me, “but the smell—it never goes away.”
I asked Ash what MAUL stands for. “It’s not initials,” he explained. “It’s a Star Wars thing—you know, Darth Maul? We’ve got a few nerds here.” The name is in all caps because the battalion’s stencil kit has only capital letters.
On the battlefield, these new machines have become priority targets for Russia’s drone pilots. They know that, for the morale of the Ukrainian crews coordinating rescues, losing a comrade in vivid detail on the monitors tracking the mission can be devastating. Russian operators wait until the wounded are loaded, then strike.
Aerial drones have created a death zone on the front lines, up to 20 miles wide, where anything caught in the open is likely to be struck. Unmanned ground vehicles began arriving in late 2024, mostly running resupply routes parallel to the front. But a mission in early 2025 proved that they could do more than this—that they were capable of reaching deep into the death zone to remove personnel. That mission began with a Facebook post.
In February 2025, near Kupiansk, Ukraine, a Russian advance trapped three Ukrainian soldiers from the 154th Mechanized Brigade behind enemy lines. All were wounded, two severely. For weeks, unit commanders attempted to pull them out. “We tried everything,” Kseniya Vynohradova, a veteran of the 154th who now leads an online support group for the unit, told me. Every effort failed.
“The brigade dropped supplies by drone,” Vynohradova told me, “but there was no way to get the guys out.” After a month of fending off Russian attacks and surviving on air-dropped rations, the soldiers were ready to give up. Their wounds had turned gangrenous, and their chance of survival was near zero. “I did not know what else to do,” Vynohradova said, “so I turned to Facebook.”
The first person to offer hope was Viktor Dolhopyatov. In a secret facility in central Ukraine, he runs Burevii, one of the country’s most innovative defense-tech companies. Russian bombardments have shattered most of the windows, but this superficial damage, common to thousands of buildings across the region, offers a kind of camouflage. From here, Burevii has transformed the modern battlefield. When Dolhopyatov read Vynohradova’s Facebook post, he answered immediately: “Tell us more, we want to help.”
Burevii’s engineers were developing a ground drone at the time. It would need a few modifications for a mission deep into the death zone—anti-drone netting, software updates, and a trailer attachment to carry three soldiers at once—but it could be ready within days. Olha Garbovskaya had joined the company two weeks prior and threw herself into the mission. “We called our machine Ardal,” she told me, after a son of the Greek god of craftsmen and technology. With engineers still attaching its final pieces, Ardal was rushed to the front.
The rescue began at dusk, with daylight fading but temperatures warm enough to partially mask Ardal’s heat signature. From a command bunker, Burevii’s engineers watched the mission unfold. High-definition screens displayed a ground’s-eye view from the drone. Overhead feeds tracked Ardal’s route to the stranded soldiers, who followed its progress over their radio. Without warning, a massive heat bloom filled the infrared monitors in the bunker. Ardal had struck a mine.
“Our hearts sank,” Garbovskaya said. “The commanders told us we had less than a 1 percent chance of succeeding, and we feared they were right.” Over the radio, the stranded men responded stoically: “We can’t take any more—just finish us off.” They begged to be bombed by Ukrainian drones. The team from Burevii asked them to hold out a little longer.
“Give us 48 hours,” Dolhopyatov said. “We have another machine.”
The second Ardal followed a different path through the minefield, and overhead bomber drones scoured the route to clear suspected mines. Ardal finally reached the men’s trench. They emerged ragged and wounded, but alive. Overhead, Russian drones closed in. From the command bunker, medics offered encouragement over the radio: “Climb in fast—we’re getting you out.”
Ardal carried them to safety, under the watchful eye of Ukrainian aerial drones. In the command bunker, Garbovskaya surveyed the scene. More than 50 people—pilots, medics, electronic warfare crews, engineers—had all assembled to save three men.
For most of history, recovering injured personnel from an active battlefield has not been a military priority. If the wounded could not make their way to safety, they were left until the fighting stopped. Serious injuries almost always ended in death, and the ratio of wounded to killed was about 3 to 1.
During the First World War, evacuating wounded soldiers became its own professionalized combat discipline. Many injuries were still fatal, but the ratio of wounded to killed began to improve. By the time of the Vietnam War, the widespread adoption of helicopters and the doctrine of the “golden hour”—the narrow window in which medical intervention is most likely to save a life—drove the survival ratio to 5 wounded for every soldier killed.
During America’s wars in Iraq and Afghanistan, rapid evacuation and advanced medical interventions brought survivability to historic highs. For every American soldier killed in those wars, approximately 10 survived their injuries. But in Ukraine, the death zone has made rapid evacuation all but impossible. Survivability has fallen, with a wounded-to-killed ratio of about 5 to 1.
Units such as the 1st Medical Battalion are trying to change that. The old battlefield math held that in many instances, rescuing a wounded soldier required more resources and risk than could be justified for a single life. But Ukraine has opted for a different way of calculating.
The military has introduced a points system that assigns varying values to different missions, rewarding units with credits that can be traded for new gear and supplies. Under the “ePoints” scheme, a routine resupply run earns two to three points; a casualty evacuation earns upwards of 70. On today’s battlefield, saving a single Ukrainian soldier is worth more than destroying a Russian tank.
Inside the death zone, Ukraine’s trenches are so difficult to reach that medics have had to reimagine the golden hour. Wound treatment must be provided on-site, by fellow soldiers. There simply are not enough medics for every trench.
Andrii Fedoryshyn, call sign “Jared,” is a trainer with the 1st Med. “The best thing we can teach a soldier is combat first aid,” he told me. “It’s more important than knowing how to shoot.”
The numbers bear this out. Less than 1 percent of the injuries seen by the 1st Med are gunshot wounds, and a soldier is far more likely to be called on to aid a buddy than to engage with the enemy. Everyone near the death zone, even journalists, carries a tourniquet. Many soldiers carry two or more, in the event that shrapnel severs multiple arteries. Once immediate care is provided, the waiting begins.
“For a front-line soldier, evacuation can take weeks,” the deputy commander of the 1st Med, who asked to be identified by only his first name, Igor, told me. “We once evac’d a patient who had a tourniquet on for 33 days.” That soldier’s unit tried everything to get him out: six attempts, six failures, and multiple armored vehicles lost in the process. The decision was made to send in a MAUL. “He lost the limb,” Igor said. “But we saved his life.”
As battlefield resources, MAULs are severely limited. Still, they are treated as expendable. Soldiers’ lives matter more. On average, two MAULs are lost for every five lives saved. I asked Ash, the battalion’s evacuation coordinator, if he ever got sentimental about the machines. “They’re tools,” he answered. “We don’t get attached.”
The platoon commander, call sign “Devi,” interrupted. “Except for this one,” he said, pulling up a video on his phone. It showed a MAUL that had lasted 10 missions, surviving drones and mines and saving the lives of 11 soldiers. After it was finally destroyed, its operators compiled a tribute video and posted it online, endowing the dead MAUL with a small but devoted fan club.
Officially, the logo of the 1st Med is a coiled snake, the ancient Greek symbol for medicine. The MAUL drivers have an unofficial logo of their own: a coffin overlaid with a progress indicator. They call themselves the “Tomb Raiders,” because, as Devi explained, “we bring people back from the dead.” Hence the movie posters plastered around the bunker, featuring Angelina Jolie in her Tomb Raider role. Opposite a wall of monitors, a scantily clad Jolie is covered in stickers featuring the coffin-and-timer logo. Each one represents a life saved. “When we fill the whole poster,” Igor explained, “we’ll auction it off to buy more machines.”
As much as medics value their MAULs, the soldiers I spoke with hated them. “No windows, no ports,” one told me. “I would rather have less protection and see what’s coming at me.” Once sealed in, a patient’s only link to the outside is a single ray of light streaming through the hinge seam and an intercom connected to the medic.
On a range far from the front, I rode inside a new MAUL undergoing testing. The coffin-like pod was stifling, and the bumpy ride nearly shook the bones out of my body. “I understand why soldiers hate it,” I told Devi. He received the feedback like a bad Yelp review. “Fair enough,” he said, “but a soldier able to complain is a soldier who survived.” The overwhelming majority of those rescued by a MAUL live to talk about it.
In the command bunker, a casualty call came in: severe internal bleeding, with developing sepsis. A MAUL set off. Overhead surveillance drones tracked its progress as the bombers scanned the route for potential mines. Ash checked in via radio about the soldier’s condition.
From the overhead feed, we saw the MAUL stop at a tree line. Two Ukrainian soldiers emerged from the foliage. One helped load the other into the sarcophagus, sealed the lid, and disappeared into the woods. Inside the command bunker, a calm professionalism prevailed. No voices were raised, except for Ash’s; he spoke loudly into his headset so that the patient could hear him over the noise of the machine.
Midway through the eight-mile return journey, the electronic-warfare team detected a heavy Russian suicide drone, a Molniya, lurking overhead. The MAUL took cover, let the Molniya pass, then continued to the transfer point where a medical team awaited. As it approached the rendezvous, the Ukrainians spotted another approaching drone. “Three kilometers, closing,” came the call. The patient was quickly lifted into an armored vehicle, which sped off toward the field hospital.
Ash’s job was done. He took off his headset and slumped into a couch. In the dim light, I noticed for the first time that he was wearing Crocs. His T-shirt, a Polish streetwear brand, said Ghosh. I sat next to him, somehow exhausted even though I had done nothing but observe. Through the walls I felt the thump of nearby drone strikes. No one else in the bunker seemed to notice them.
I asked Ash what he did before the war. “Musical theater,” he said. “I was a performer.” I asked about his greatest fear as a combat medic. “Losing one of our guys en route,” he answered. Not seeing the gore of injuries, or wondering whether his bunker would be hit. His heaviest burden was the thought of a disabled MAUL, one of his patients trapped inside, unable to make it home.
“Has this ever happened?” I asked.
“Yes,” he said. “Twice.”
In the Russian military, by contrast, being wounded and abandoned is the norm. At a POW camp in western Ukraine, I spoke with several Russian prisoners of war. “I was wounded in the legs,” one prisoner, who asked that I withhold his name for fear of reprisal, told me. “There was no rescue—my own guys left me to die.”
The first medical attention he received was from the Ukrainian military. Reliable figures for Russia’s wounded-to-killed ratio are difficult to pin down, but conservative estimates place it at about 2 to 1, worse than the survival ratio of Russian soldiers during World War I.
At the foothills of Ukraine’s Carpathian Mountains, far from the front lines, lies a rehab facility for injured soldiers. I met Pavlo there, four months into his recovery from injuries sustained trying to rescue another soldier. He had successfully driven his truck to the pickup point for his wounded comrade when he was struck by a Russian drone. Shrapnel entered his abdomen, tore through his bladder, and broke his pelvis. Someone dragged him into a trench. Pavlo begged to stay there, remembering the wrecked and burning vehicles littering the road he drove in on. Over the radio, the medics insisted, “If you do not leave, you will die for sure.”
At dusk, the unmanned ground vehicle came. Over the next three hours, the teams behind it—medics, ground-drone operators, bomber- and aerial-surveillance-drone pilots, and electronic-warfare crews—performed the intricate choreography needed to carry Pavlo to safety.
From the top of a Carpathian ski resort, under a cloud-dappled sky, Pavlo recounted every detail, from his failed attempt to rescue his fellow soldier to the moment he went into surgery. Every few minutes, we glanced skyward to scan for threats. We were safe, but such habits die hard. Pavlo would soon return to his new wife, and he knew that this would have been impossible without the ground drone and the humans who operated it, all working together to save this one soldier.
“I never met them,” Pavlo said. “A robot carried me, but people saved me. So many, just for me.”
He looked up again. “I don’t even know their names.”

articles.title: A drone came down beside a Bundeswehr air base, weeks after Berlin blamed Moscow for the Leipzig airport attack
articles.body:
A large-scale police operation is underway after a drone of unknown origin crashed 1 kilometer from a Bundeswehr base, German media outlet Bild reported on 15 September.
Drones have repeatedly flown over German military bases, and German prosecutors are already treating one August find near Ukraine-bound cargo as attempted sabotage. Germany's military counterintelligence has tied repeated sabotage on German soil to Russia, with high probability. Neither the owner nor the origin of this drone is known. Russia has denied involvement in earlier incidents, some of which Germany has officially attributed to it.
Discovery near airbase triggers large-scale search
Parts of the drone were found east of Lake Steinhude, the media outlet said. The crash site is one kilometer from the Bundeswehr's Wunstorf air base in Lower Saxony, the German military confirmed to the outlet. The drone crashed in an open, uninhabited area, the state criminal police office said. After the debris was discovered, authorities launched a large-scale search operation in the area to find additional parts of the UAV, according to Bild.
Investigators do not yet know who owns the drone
The search continues, and the state criminal police office says there are so far no indications of a danger to the public. Investigators learned about the discovery on Monday and want to analyze any other drone parts they find to determine its origin, the media outlet reported. Only then could more be said about the circumstances of the crash, it added.
Germany will close Russia’s Bonn consulate after attributing Leipzig Airport drone attack to Moscow
Drones have been spotted over Bundeswehr bases many times
Since the beginning of the full-scale invasion, the number of reports of drone sightings has "increased significantly" and become "more consistent," a spokesperson for the Bundeswehr Operations Command told RedaktionsNetzwerk Deutschland (RND) in August.
"Overall, several hundred suspected drone overflights have been reported in the area of the German Armed Forces in recent years," the command spokesperson told RND.
What came before this crash
Germany is the busiest front in Russia's covert campaign in Europe. A Semtex-laden drone turned up beside a Ukrainian cargo plane at Leipzig/Halle airport in August, and investigators this month named a Russian intelligence operative and a Belarusian petty criminal. Berlin blamed Moscow and ordered Russia's Bonn consulate closed.
Two Bulgarians were arrested over a September arson at a Munich building site between two defense-tech headquarters, a day after two attempts to sabotage the power grid that Germany has not attributed. Germany suspects a planned assassination of a Bavarian drone maker's boss, watched by agents hired for single jobs.
The throwaway agents Moscow sent after a Bavarian drone boss arming Ukraine—and how Germany stopped them
Not every strand leads to Moscow. German military counterintelligence this week attributed part of the drone activity over Bundeswehr sites to Chinese intelligence.
Elsewhere the tempo holds: Polish prosecutors have opened more than a hundred espionage cases in 20 months, and in the Netherlands a former commander of US Army forces in Europe said Russian saboteurs attacked the rail network and tried to kill him, which Dutch Railways said they knew nothing about.

articles.title: Germans who opted for alternative civilian service once went to help vulnerable people in countries devastated by the Nazis, including Russia and Belarus. Then Moscow started a new war in Europe.
articles.body:
Germans who opted for alternative civilian service once went to help vulnerable people in countries devastated by the Nazis, including Russia and Belarus. Then Moscow started a new war in Europe.
From 1990 through the 2000s, Germans traveled to Russia and several other countries to perform alternative civilian service. German women came too, but as volunteers. They worked in hospitals, residential facilities for people with mental and neurological disabilities, and other care homes, and helped older people in their homes. One motivation was to atone for their ancestors’ guilt during World War II, seek reconciliation with the peoples who had suffered under Nazi Germany, and do something useful for them. Meduza spoke with volunteers from those years and the organizers behind the initiative.
In the mid-1980s, pacifist organizations took Germany’s alternative civilian service program abroad
After World War II, West Germany had no armed forces of its own. It did not begin establishing them until the mid-1950s, and a military service law was adopted in 1956. At the same time, West Germany’s constitution enshrined the right to refuse military service on grounds of conscience and perform alternative civilian service instead. This service had to benefit society in some way and was performed in hospitals, nursing homes, and other social care institutions.
An army began taking shape in East Germany at around the same time. But unarmed service was not permitted until 1964. Men who refused to bear arms on religious or other grounds could then serve in construction units known as construction battalions. This was not a civilian alternative in the West German sense: members of the construction battalions remained military personnel and wore uniforms, but were not issued weapons. They could be assigned to build defense installations and other military facilities.
For many years, proving one’s pacifist convictions in West Germany was extremely difficult. The process became easier in the 1980s, and officials realized that people seeking alternative civilian service could provide cheap labor. The number of people entering alternative civilian service rose sharply. Eventually, Sergey Krivenko, a board member of the International Memorial Association, told Meduza, German pacifist organizations secured permission for participants to perform this service abroad.
One of these organizations was Action Reconciliation Service for Peace (ASF). Founded in the late 1950s, it later helped men perform alternative civilian service abroad in countries that had suffered under Nazi aggression. ASF also recruited men and women seeking volunteer experience for projects abroad.
“ASF and other organizations began looking for local groups that could arrange this kind of volunteer work,” Sergey Krivenko said. “In other words, it wasn’t done through the government but through NGOs [nonprofit organizations]. In the early 1990s, a special center called Compassion was established within Moscow Memorial to help former victims of political repression. Those were hard times, with everything falling apart. Social services were only just being established. Most of the work was like this: older people lived alone and needed someone to clean, cook, and go shopping for them. The idea came up to bring in volunteers from [ASF and other organizations] to do this work. And it worked.”
The German initiatives also established contacts with other NGOs, churches, and residential institutions, sending volunteers to work with them.
In her book “Nestrashny mir” (“A World Without Fear”), special education teacher Maria Berkovich says that at the children’s home near St. Petersburg where she began volunteering in the 2000s, all volunteers were called Germans because there had never been any others:
The first German volunteers came to the children’s home more than 10 years ago. Ever since then, they have come every year and stayed for a year; when their term ends, new volunteers replace them. The organization also has ties to a German school for occupational therapists, so every year two or three of the school’s graduates come to the children’s home for six months to work with the children… Tanya, Sveta, and I became the first Russian volunteers at this children’s home.
The director of a St. Petersburg foundation that helped children and adults in residential institutions told anthropologist Anna Klepikova that when volunteers began working at the children’s home, few staff members saw any point in it. Klepikova quotes her in the book “Naverno, ya durak” (“I Must Be an Idiot”):
Most people thought we were wasting our time on nonsense. They told me point-blank, ‘Sure, you can tell the Germans whatever you want to get money out of them, but you and I understand that these children don’t need anything, right? And that they can’t develop, right?’ I think that if it hadn’t been a German organization, it simply wouldn’t have happened, because Russians who suddenly started working with children like these would have been seen as idiots. That’s all there is to it.
Hundreds of volunteers came to Russia — most of them without knowing Russian
The German volunteers who spoke with Meduza said the organizations that sent them paid for their trips. The program was funded not by the government but through donations collected by civic organizations. These funds could be used to rent shared apartments for volunteers and cover food, transportation, and other basic expenses.
Sergey Krivenko said Germans worked in at least Moscow, St. Petersburg, Volgograd, and Perm in Russia, as well as Minsk in Belarus. Their numbers were not especially large: Moscow, for example, might have hosted 10–20 volunteers a year. In all, hundreds of young people from Germany spent time in Russia and Belarus over the years.
Sergey Krivenko gave Meduza his overall impression of the German volunteers he met in the late 1990s and the 2000s:
They were incredibly interesting young men and women. [Some of them] were part of the volunteer ”social year” program. But of course they were young and wanted to have fun. After all, this kind of work was a chance to travel somewhere for free, and an adventure too. They also had strong ideological motivation: we’re doing a good thing, helping people. […] Sometimes we met some very interesting characters. One, for example, was the grandson of an SS general. He made a conscious decision to go to Russia to repay his family’s debt, as he saw it.
The volunteers studied the language while they worked. Many of Meduza’s interviewees said they were supposed to take a two-week intensive Russian course in Germany before leaving. Some spoke positively about the course; others did not. Either way, they had to overcome the language barrier once they arrived.
“They came without knowing Russian,” Sergey Krivenko said. “And within the first three months, through their contact with victims of political repression… they began to speak and understand it reasonably well. It was amazing.”
Young men doing alternative civilian service came to Russia from the early 1990s through the late 2000s. Germany abolished compulsory military service in 2011 and shifted to a professional army, reducing the number of German citizens working in social care institutions. Even so, volunteers continued coming to post-Soviet countries to do charitable work.
‘I have so many memories that usually shock people’
“If you have no connection to Russia, you don’t pay attention to what the media reports about it,” one German volunteer said in an interview with the charity Perspektivy. “Of course, I had a general picture in my head: freezing winters, Red Square, Moscow, St. Basil’s Cathedral, a samovar. All the usual clichés. Growing up in East Germany, I encountered the ‘big brother’ from the Soviet Union in kindergarten and at school, but even so, I had no idea what Russia was really like. I even bought a kettle back then and brought it to Russia because I didn’t know whether I’d be able to buy one there.”
Sofia came to Russia in the early 1990s. She told Meduza that her work had been arranged through a Moscow church:
A priest met us and arranged for us to stay in his nephew’s apartment. It had three rooms: the nephew lived there, and the five of us got the other two rooms. Four boys and me. We had fun, but I got away from them pretty quickly. I was from East Germany, and they were from West Germany. We could communicate easily, but they were too Western for me. And I realized I wouldn’t learn Russian if I stayed with them.”
With help from the Orthodox community, Sofia then found a home with a local family. The host church also arranged volunteer placements for her and the other young people. They mostly helped older people in their homes:
I had to buy groceries, and I learned to make porridge. Cleaning too. It was very nice. I met some remarkable people. One was a former Russian teacher who would sit with me and teach me the language. There was also a former cosmonaut who told me how he had been made to stand on his head for long periods and how they had conducted some kind of terrible experiments on him.
Volunteers could also help at one of Moscow’s residential institutions in their free time if they wished. Sofia said about 50 children of all ages lived there, from infants to teenagers approaching adulthood. Because the facility was understaffed, some of the children were often tied to their beds. “It was a very sad sight,” Sofia said. “The home had children with severe illnesses, as well as orphans who acted as caregivers for the sick children. I tried to teach them English and German. I was just a volunteer — I saw what needed doing, and I did it.”
Another volunteer, Matteo, performed his alternative service in Minsk through ASF in the mid-2000s. He said he became interested in Russian while still in school, thanks to a Ukrainian friend of his father’s. Alternative service in the former Soviet Union therefore seemed like an appealing option. Matteo was assigned to a children’s residential institution in the Minsk neighborhood of Navinki. He also spent some time helping adults at a residential facility for people with mental and neurological disabilities in the city’s Drazhnya neighborhood. Matteo said:
I still remember the stench in the hallways [at the institution in Navinki]. I have so many memories that usually shock people, yet by the end of the conversation, you’re left feeling that the person you’re talking to still hasn’t really understood. Because they never lived in that system.
There was one very withdrawn autistic boy who usually stood in a corner and sometimes hit himself. By the end of the year, I could communicate with him and was the only person who could calm him down. I was proud of that at the time. But at the end of the year, I told him I was leaving. He hit me and himself very hard. When I came back for a couple of days six months later, he was just as withdrawn as ever. Who knows whether that means it was all for nothing. Or maybe it wasn’t…”
Matteo also told Meduza about the institution in Drazhnya:
