For me, Drazhnya was darker than Navinki. The building was bigger, and I usually stayed in the first two rooms on the ground floor. Four young women with cerebral palsy lived there; they had previously been at the institution in Navinki. Farther down, in the shadows of the hallway, there were beds and wheelchairs with people in them, amid moans and a stench. And there was a television mounted on the ceiling, with two or three orderlies sitting around it. I only found the courage a couple of times to ask someone from the hallway to go for a walk outside. I usually preferred the comfort and familiarity of those first two rooms.
Matteo said that he and the women who lived in the first two rooms would usually go for walks, talk, drink tea, smoke, go shopping, dye their hair, and listen to music. “We had a friendly relationship, but naturally, it wasn’t entirely equal,” Matteo said. “Unlike in Navinki, they had their own lockers and even cellphones. They often called to ask when we were coming back. Sometimes they messaged so often that it got annoying.”
Anthropologist Anna Klepikova’s book “Naverno, ya durak” (“I Must Be an Idiot”) includes a foundation director’s account of how difficult it was to find volunteers for an adult residential institution in St. Petersburg: “Volunteers fainted, and we had to send the German volunteers home because they couldn’t handle working in the adult institution.” According to the director, volunteers found it easy to imagine themselves in the adult residents’ place and picture themselves living in the same “utterly inhuman conditions.”
“We spent three years fighting just to get the residents spoons, for example,” the foundation director said. “There were no spoons, and they lapped food out of bowls like dogs. And the smells — when we first arrived at the residential facility for people with mental and neurological disabilities, it was absolutely horrifying. People lay there all day, wet and covered in filth, in pain that no one paid any attention to.”
Like Matteo, a volunteer named Emma worked in Minsk, though she came in the 2010s. She decided to volunteer immediately after finishing school, before enrolling at a university. Emma’s mother was a historian, and Emma said Germany’s history had mattered to her since childhood:
When you realize that you’re German, what that may mean to other people, what grievances they may have — entirely justified grievances… It was important to me to do this work.
Our hosts in Minsk had lists of former prisoners of concentration camps and other Nazi camps, including elderly women who had been forced to work in Germany. We visited them to help. We went shopping and cleaned for them. But they were always fussing over us and feeding us. It was very nice.
I also worked at a center for children with various kinds of cancer. We just played with them, made things out of clay, and drew pictures. I remember spending a lot of time with one girl who was seven or eight years old and lived in isolation in a separate room. You couldn’t simply walk in to see her. You needed a mask and shoe covers. I played with her so her mother could get some rest.
‘Our volunteer service was in the cause of peace. And now there was a new war’
The institutions’ overall atmosphere did not strike the volunteers who spoke with Meduza as “a horror movie with no escape.”
Although conditions in the social care institutions were difficult, Sofia said the people around her were very curious during her time there, and it was easy to become part of the local community. Everyone was intrigued: “Some Germans have come here to volunteer.” People wanted to support the young volunteers who had come to help.
One volunteer told the charity Perspektivy that he ate nothing but bread and butter for his first few weeks: “Back then, every store still had those separate departments, and without knowing Russian, it was almost impossible to buy anything. It took some time, but human relationships are always what matters most. And because our relationships with people were good, I felt comfortable and quickly got used to everything. We were a good team, and people took good care of us.”
Meduza’s interviewees said they made many local friends and stayed in touch with them for years. As a result, after volunteering, Sofia, Emma, and Matteo all returned more than once to Moscow, Minsk, and other cities in the former Soviet Union.
In early 2022, Emma flew to Russia as an exchange student studying medicine. Her program lasted around six months, so she was in Moscow when Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine:
Our earlier volunteer service was in the cause of peace. We felt guilty, and it took decades before we were able to come as volunteers to countries that had suffered during World War II. And now there was a new war.
If I had known in advance, I wouldn’t have gone at all. Everything became clear only on February 21–22. I’ll never forget those days. I don’t think the other German exchange students felt the way I did, because they hadn’t had my experience or grappled with the subject of war the way I had. And I couldn’t find the words [to explain it all to them]. In those circumstances, with all that propaganda, and especially as a German, a “daughter of fascists,” it wasn’t easy.
Following Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine, Emma volunteered at Moscow’s Sakharov Center in her free time until her exchange program ended in the summer of 2022.
At Meduza, we are committed to transparency about our use of artificial intelligence in the newsroom. The story you’re reading was written by one of our living, breathing journalists and translated from Russian using an AI model configured to follow our strict editorial standards. This translation process is the result of extensive testing and refinements to ensure our English-language coverage is timely and accurate. A Meduza editor reviews every draft before publication.
If you find any errors in this translation, please contact us at [email protected].
To read Meduza’s exclusive content in English, please subscribe to our newsletter.

articles.title: Poland scrambles fighter jets and closes Lublin and Rzeszów airports in response to Russian attacks on Ukraine
articles.body:
Poland scrambles fighter jets and closes Lublin and Rzeszów airports in response to Russian attacks on Ukraine
Due to the need to ensure airspace security, operations at the airports in Lublin and Rzeszów were temporarily restricted.
This was reported by the Polish Armed Forces Operational Command and the Polish Government Security Center, according to Ukrinform.
The Polish Armed Forces Operational Command reported on social media platform X that, in connection with Russian strikes on Ukraine, the Polish Air Force had begun operations in the country’s airspace. At the same time, ground-based air defense and radar reconnaissance systems were placed on alert. The command emphasized that these measures were preventive in nature and aimed at protecting Polish airspace.
Subsequently, the Operational Command announced the completion of the military aviation operation related to the Russian strikes on Ukraine. Ground-based air defense and radar reconnaissance systems returned to standard operations. According to military officials, no violations of Polish airspace were recorded.
Residents of the Lublin and Województwo podkarpackie in Poland received text messages from the Government Security Center alerting them to the emergency and military aviation operations in the airspace.
Due to military aviation activity, operations at the airports in Lublin and Rzeszów were temporarily suspended. The restrictions were in place for a short time, after which airport operations resumed.
As reported by Ukrinform, an enemy drone struck a bus in the Nikopol region. Five people were killed and seven were injured.
Illustrative photo: Wikipedia

articles.title: EU Chief Pledges Strongest-Ever Winter Support and Air Defense for Ukraine
articles.body:
- Category
- World
EU Chief Pledges Strongest-Ever Winter Support and Air Defense for Ukraine
European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen pledged to provide Ukraine with its strongest-ever support package to help the nation navigate the harsh upcoming winter during her annual State of the European Union address to the European Parliament on September 16.
“Together with our partners, we will provide humanitarian aid and strengthen Ukraine’s supply of electricity and heat,” von der Leyen stated, emphasizing the critical need to fortify the country’s decentralized power grid and centralized heating systems against Russian aerial bombardment.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
She added that the European Union would also rapidly expand its support for Ukrainian air defenses.
The European Commission president underscored the urgent necessity of accelerating the delivery of American Patriot interceptor missiles to Kyiv. However, she also stressed the strategic importance of curbing the continent’s dependence on single-source military suppliers.
To achieve this, von der Leyen announced that Brussels and Kyiv are collaborating to engineer an “affordable modular missile-defense platform.” A key element of this joint initiative is Project FREYJA, which aims to pair Ukrainian combat experience with European industrial manufacturing to build a sustainable, homegrown air defense network.
Project FREYJA is a pan-European, multi-layered anti-ballistic missile defense initiative designed to create an affordable, open-architecture alternative to interceptor systems, similar to the US Patriot. Initiated by Ukraine and backed by a coalition of ten European nations, the project integrates NATO-standard radars with domestic interceptors to build a decentralized continental shield capable of neutralizing Russian ballistic threats.
Looking beyond immediate battlefield requirements, von der Leyen outlined a wider geopolitical vision by pitching the creation of a “European Security Council.” Under this proposed framework, EU leaders would establish an emergency security protocol to regularly convene with the heads of key partner states—specifically naming Canada, Norway, Ukraine, and the United Kingdom—to address hybrid threats and coordinate continental defense.
EU High Representative Kaja Kallas had recently warned that the rise of far-right political movements, such as Alternative for Germany, threatens to undermine continental defense against Moscow. As Kremlin sabotage and hybrid operations draw closer to EU borders, Kallas cautioned that parties taking a passive stance on Russian aggression are creating dangerous security blind spots across Europe.
Discuss this article:

articles.title: Ukrainian partisans claim sabotage at Russian plant supplying missiles Moscow uses to bomb Ukrainian cities
articles.body:
Pro-Ukrainian partisan movement ATESH says it sabotaged the power supply to a Russian semiconductor plant in Voronezh that produces electronic components used in Russia’s missiles and air defense systems.
Targeting such suppliers can hit Russia’s ability to sustain its missile campaign: disrupting production of critical electronic components can slow the replenishment of weapons used to strike Ukrainian cities.
In a statement published on 16 September, ATESH said one of its agents infiltrated an electrical substation near the Voronezh Semiconductor Devices Plant-Sborka (VZPP-S) and destroyed the main distribution cabinet supplying the facility. The movement said the agent escaped the city after the operation.
VZPP-S is a Russian producer of semiconductor devices, integrated circuits and power modules. Ukraine’s military intelligence lists the company as part of Russia’s defense-industrial supply chain and says it has produced electronic components for Kh-101 cruise missiles, Iskander-K missiles and Pantsir-S1 air defense systems.
ATESH claimed the sabotage caused a major voltage surge and shut down production workshops. The movement said full power was not restored for several weeks, causing delays in deliveries of components for Russian weapons and, consequently, delays in missile and air defense production.
The movement’s claims have not been independently verified.
ATESH is a pro-Ukrainian partisan movement operating in Russian-occupied territories and inside Russia. It says it recruits local residents and Russian military personnel to conduct sabotage, gather intelligence and pass information to Ukraine. The movement regularly publishes claims of attacks and acts of sabotage against Russian military and defense-industrial targets, though individual operations are often difficult to independently verify.
The plant has already been targeted
The reported sabotage comes after the VZPP-S facility was struck in a Ukrainian attack in June.
Ukraine’s military intelligence says VZPP-S produces components for the Kh-101, including transistor assemblies and matrices used in the missile’s electronic systems. It also says the company supplies semiconductor components for the onboard computer of the 9M727 cruise missile used by the Iskander-K system, as well as components for the Pantsir-S1’s television channel.
The company itself describes VZPP-S as a major Russian producer of electronic components, with more than 900 products in serial production.
ATESH said it delayed publication of its claim to protect its agent.

articles.title: Germany to send fighter jets to Latvia during election amid drone threat
articles.body:
Two Eurofighter jets of the German Air Force fly through the sky over the air base in Wittmund, northeastern Germany. | Focke Strangmann/AFP via Getty Images
BERLIN — Germany will deploy Eurofighter jets to Latvia to help protect its airspace during next month’s parliamentary election as repeated drone incursions have raised security concerns along NATO’s eastern flank.
Four German Eurofighters will be sent to the Lielvārde Air Base in central Latvia for about a week from late September into early October, Germany’s defense ministry said Wednesday. The ministry added that Latvia had requested additional support from its NATO allies to secure its airspace ahead of the Oct. 3 vote.
The Latvian defense ministry did not immediately respond to POLITICO’s request for comment.
Advertisement
Latvia has experienced several drone incidents this year. NATO fighters shot down a foreign drone over the east of the country in June, while another drone was destroyed in August. Authorities later said the August aircraft was Ukrainian and had likely entered Latvian airspace from Belarus after being affected by Russian electronic warfare.
Latvia’s defense ministry has warned that further foreign drones could infringe on its airspace as long as Russia’s war against Ukraine continues.
The German jets, from Tactical Air Wing 74 in Neuburg an der Donau, will operate under NATO’s enhanced Air Policing North mission, which forms part of the alliance’s integrated air and missile defense system. Germany will also deploy several dozen personnel.
Germany separately announced that five Eurofighters and around 120 troops will deploy to Ämari in Estonia from December through March for a regular NATO air policing rotation. That will be Germany’s seventh such mission to that part of Estonia.

articles.title: Poland plans to provide Patriot missiles to Ukraine: Report
articles.body:
Şeyma Erkul Dayanç
16 September 2026•Update: 16 September 2026
Poland plans to provide Ukraine with several PAC-3 interceptor missiles for US-made Patriot air defense systems as part of a new military aid package, Polish broadcaster TVP reported Wednesday.
The planned package is expected to be worth about €50 million ($58 million) and focus largely on air defense capabilities, according to Ukraine's Defense Ministry.
Poland's Defense Ministry has confirmed that a new military support package is being prepared but has not disclosed the equipment it will contain, citing official secrecy.
The ministry told daily Rzeczpospolita that the package would include equipment being withdrawn from service by the Polish Armed Forces because its service life is expiring.
The equipment would no longer be used by Poland but could still be useful to Ukraine, the ministry said.
PAC-3 interceptors for Poland's Patriot systems are among the equipment being considered for transfer, according to sources familiar with the preparations.
Poland's operational commander, Maj. Gen. Ireneusz Nowak, said he supported providing Ukraine with Patriot ammunition but indicated that the number of missiles would be limited.
“No one is talking about mass donations,” he said.
Poland provided Ukraine with five PAC-3 missiles in July.
Ukraine has repeatedly asked its allies for additional air defense munitions as it seeks to replenish its stocks amid continued Russian missile and drone attacks.
Kyiv has specifically emphasized the need for PAC-3 interceptors ahead of an expected Russian winter campaign targeting civilian and energy infrastructure.
Polish Defense Minister Wladyslaw Kosiniak-Kamysz said in July that Poland had provided Ukraine with about €3.8 billion ($4.4 billion) in military aid.

articles.title: Taiwan military launches Patriot missiles in joint precision weapons drill
articles.body:
TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — The military launched Patriot missiles and other major weapons Wednesday morning as it began a multi-day joint precision weapons exercise at Jiupeng Military Base in Pingtung County.
The drill is designed to test the military’s long-range precision strike capabilities and the performance of newly acquired missiles, rockets, and attack drones, per Liberty Times. Four major weapon systems took part in the opening phase before dawn.
The opening phase focused on air defense and air-to-air systems, testing unit deployment and command-and-control links. The launches demonstrated the military’s ability to respond rapidly to aerial threats.
The Tien Kung air defense missile system, HIMARS multiple launch rocket systems, and land-based Sky Sword II missiles are scheduled to take part in subsequent phases, Liberty Times reported. Coast Guard vessels will also launch Hsiung Feng-series anti-ship missiles as part of the exercise.
The Defense Ministry has invited President Lai Ching-te (賴清德) to observe the exercise. The drill is intended to assess the military’s and the Coast Guard’s ability to conduct joint operations during wartime.

articles.title: The EU is militarizing the Arctic. Here’s how it plans to do it
articles.body:
The EU is militarizing the Arctic. Here’s how it plans to do it
The EU’s Arctic policy is becoming increasingly important amidst global competition driven by both climate change and the region’s strategic significance. Melting Arctic ice is opening new maritime transport routes, facilitating access to abundant natural resources, and creating conditions for expanded economic activity. Consequently, the Arctic is becoming an arena for rivalry among the leading global powers. For Brussels, the Arctic holds not only regional significance but is also a tool for achieving foreign policy and geopolitical objectives.
Adopted in October 2021, the EU’s current Arctic policy is titled ‘A stronger EU engagement for a peaceful, sustainable and prosperous Arctic’. It focuses on three ‘soft’ priorities: climate and environmental protection, sustainable development, and peace and cooperation. Essentially, in this document, the Arctic is viewed as a low-tension zone, and the primary focus is on the environment and scientific exchange.
However, a lot has changed in the world since 2021, from the Ukraine crisis to the paralysis of the Arctic Council, Trump’s bid to acquire Greenland, Chinese container ships traveling via the Northern Sea Route, and attacks on undersea cables in the Baltic Sea. In January 2026, at the Arctic Frontiers conference in Tromsø, Norway, Kaja Kallas said, “It is time for a fresh EU Arctic policy, one that reflects the times we live in.”
A new phase of the EU’s Arctic agenda after 2022
The EU Arctic policy stands at the intersection of geopolitical, economic, and environmental interests. In recent years, Brussels has sought to adapt its strategy to the shifting international landscape shaped by a sanctions-driven confrontation with Russia, China’s expanding regional presence, and the growing role of the US in security matters. The Ukraine conflict and the region’s growing militarization have pushed the EU to revise its Arctic agenda. The EU must shape its Arctic policy by balancing a normative agenda focused on sustainable development against tangible economic interests and security demands from NATO allies.
In July 2025, the president of the European Commission announced a revision of the EU’s Arctic strategy to ensure that it addresses new challenges. Meanwhile, the EU is strengthening cooperation in the fields of energy, raw materials, and security and defense partnerships with several non-EU Arctic nations – notably Canada, Iceland, Norway, and self-governing Greenland.
Historically, Europe’s cooperation with the Arctic states has developed along three key lines: economic engagement (energy, transport infrastructure, and resource extraction), the environmental agenda (climate change, sustainable development, and biodiversity conservation), and scientific research (meteorological and oceanographic studies, as well as research on glacial melting). However, the current geopolitical situation has significantly altered these areas of cooperation, particularly when it comes to relations with Russia.
The EU joined other Arctic Council member states and “key like-minded partners” in suspending Russia’s participation in various regional cooperation bodies following the start of the war in Ukraine in 2022. Consequently, the EU issued three joint statements concerning the Northern Dimension joint policy, the Barents Euro-Arctic Council, and the Council of the Baltic Sea States. On November 12, 2025, the European Parliament adopted a new resolution on the Arctic that addresses the buildup of military capabilities and emphasizes the need for cooperation with Northern European partners (including Norway) to prepare for the upcoming geopolitical competition in the region. The resolution was passed by an overwhelming majority, with 510 votes in favor, 75 against, and 80 abstentions.
The resolution outlines a comprehensive strategy for the EU’s diplomatic engagement in the Arctic, covering areas such as environmental protection and security. The adopted document signals a shift in Brussels’ Arctic policy, envisions deeper cooperation with Arctic states, particularly Norway, and underscores the region’s significance for Europe’s energy security and geopolitical stability.
To safeguard European interests – including freedom of navigation, the protection of maritime infrastructure, and environmental security – the European Parliament calls for active cooperation with NATO, joint exercises, and coordinated surveillance and defense efforts.
Furthermore, the EU Parliament encourages multilateral governance in the Arctic through the Arctic Council and regional forums; this includes supporting efforts to grant the EU permanent observer status, engaging with Arctic institutions (such as the Arctic Economic Council), and expanding its presence in the region (for example, by means of the recently opened EU office in Nuuk).
The resolution also reaffirms the Arctic’s status as a region of strategic importance to the EU (considering its direct impact on European security), and notes that the EU must move beyond the concept of ‘Arctic exceptionalism’ and integrate High North priorities into its broader foreign, security, and energy policy strategies.
By adopting this resolution, the EU Parliament has signaled that the Arctic is no longer a remote outpost but a strategic frontier vital to Europe’s energy supply, security, digital infrastructure, and environmental sustainability.
The next step will be to integrate this non-legislative resolution into the EU’s updated Arctic policy. A step toward this was taken at the EU Arctic Summit, held September 13-14, 2026, in Rovaniemi, the capital of Finnish Lapland.
Key outcomes and decisions of the EU Arctic Summit
The summit was attended by German Chancellor Friedrich Merz, Finnish Prime Minister Petteri Orpo, EU High Representative for Foreign Affairs Kaja Kallas, European Council President António Costa, the heads of government of Denmark, Estonia, Latvia, Lithuania, and Romania, and representatives of France, Greece, the Netherlands, Poland, and Sweden.
The primary goal of the meeting, convened at the initiative of the Finnish prime minister, was to formulate a common EU strategic approach to the Arctic, a region that has become critically important to European security.
Following the EU Arctic Summit, a joint communiqué was adopted, outlining the path toward an updated EU Arctic strategy set to be presented in October 2026. Key highlights of the document include:
1) Adoption of a new Arctic strategy. Kaja Kallas announced the preparation of an updated Arctic strategy, set to be presented in October. Security takes center stage in this strategy; in her view, Russia’s growing military activity and China’s strategic investments in the Arctic compel the EU to shift toward ensuring collective defense. The participants of the summit urged the EU to maintain a more active strategic presence in the region. EU Council President António Costa stated that the increase in military spending in the Arctic would be factored into the next long-term EU budget.
2) A unified EU icebreaker fleet. The concept of jointly owning an EU icebreaker fleet was reflected in the adopted communiqué. Kallas spoke of the need to create such a fleet in light of climate change and the geopolitical situation. Finland proposed building the vessels at its own shipyards, leveraging its expertise in the field and sharing experience.
3) Investments in cross-border infrastructure. The participants emphasized the need to develop infrastructure capable of serving civilian purposes (such as supplying remote settlements) and facilitating the rapid deployment of troops. Leaders called for increased investment in military mobility, cross-border transport links, satellite infrastructure, and other facilities in the North. The discussion focused on allocating funds to reinforce roads, railways, and bridges in Finland, Sweden, and Norway – ensuring they can withstand the weight of heavy NATO armored vehicles in extreme cold – as well as modernizing deep-water ports in Northern Norway and setting up POL storage warehouses along the Barents Sea coast. The summit supported the expansion of the European satellite constellation to facilitate navigation and maritime surveillance.
4) Balancing priorities. The statement noted that, despite the strong emphasis on security, issues like climate protection, sustainable development, and peaceful cooperation remain among the priorities of the EU’s Arctic strategy. Particular importance was placed on the situation of indigenous peoples and the need to cooperate with local communities in developing the region.
5) Hybrid threats. Finland’s Petteri Orpo noted that while climate change is opening up new shipping routes, it simultaneously renders the region vulnerable to hybrid influence. The document underscored the need to enhance capabilities for responding to such challenges.
Overall, the summit in Rovaniemi marked a fundamental shift in how European leaders approach the northern territories. The Arctic is no longer seen as an environmental conservation zone and has been officially recognized as a front line in the geopolitical confrontation.
Moreover, the Arctic is no longer discussed as an isolated region; it is being integrated into what analysts call the ‘Northeastern arc’ of European security policy.
Overall, the EU’s forthcoming updated Arctic policy represents an attempt to transform the Arctic from merely an ‘environmental issue’ into an integral component of the European strategy on security, economy, and technological autonomy.

articles.title: Responsible for supplying weapons to the occupiers: Russian Deputy Defense Minister Krivoruchko was charged in absentia
articles.body:
Responsible for supplying weapons to the occupiers: Russian Deputy Defense Minister Krivoruchko was charged in absentia
Kyiv • UNN
The Russian officer is accused of waging an aggressive war against Ukraine. He organized the supply of missiles, aerial bombs, and drones to the Russian army.
Prosecutors from the Office of the Prosecutor General have completed the pretrial investigation and referred to court an indictment against Russian Deputy Defense Minister Alexey Krivoruchko. He is suspected of waging an aggressive war or aggressive military actions, as provided for by Part 2 of Article 437 of the Criminal Code of Ukraine, UNN reports, citing the Office of the Prosecutor General.
Details
According to the investigation, Krivoruchko formulated and implemented the aggressor state's military-technical policy, organized the fulfillment of the state defense order, and controlled the supply of weapons.
It was established that Krivoruchko signed state contracts for the production and supply of Kinzhal hypersonic missiles, Iskander-M missile systems, guided aerial bombs, as well as Geran- and Gerbera-type drones. He also controlled the fulfillment of defense orders and reported to the leadership of the Russian Defense Ministry on the expansion of weapons production and supplies for the Russian army
In addition, according to the investigation, the defendant initiated the creation of the Rubicon Center for Advanced Unmanned Technologies. Its units subsequently took a direct part in combat operations against Ukraine.
The evidence collected indicates that the weapons whose supply was organized and controlled by the accused were used by Russian forces during missile and drone attacks on Ukrainian territory, in particular against civilian and critical infrastructure. As a result of such attacks, civilians were killed and injured, and residential buildings and critical infrastructure facilities were destroyed
The article provides for a sentence of 10 to 15 years in prison.
Reminder
The Security Service of Ukraine and the prosecutor's office notified Russian Colonel General Sergei Kuzovlyov in absentia of suspicion over the strike on Kramatorsk in June 2023.

articles.title: Russian Forces Target Kyiv-Mykolaiv Passenger Train as 80 Drones Attack Ukraine Overnight
articles.body:
Russian forces attacked train No. 122, traveling from Kyiv to Mykolaiv, on Wednesday, Sept. 16, according to Ukrzaliznytsia.
“The enemy continues to target passenger trains. Thanks to an early warning from the Ukrzaliznytsia monitoring team, the locomotive and train crews, as well as the passengers, were evacuated,” the company said.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
Ukrzaliznytsia added that no injuries were reported. Bus transfers for passengers are being organized in cooperation with the Mykolaiv Regional Military Administration (OVA).
Meanwhile, explosions were heard in Kyiv shortly before 8 a.m. following a drone threat alert.
Kyiv Mayor Vitali Klitschko later reported that one person was injured when unmanned aerial vehicle (UAV) debris fell on warehouse premises in the Sviatoshynskyi district. The injured person was hospitalized.
However, it remains unclear whether these were the result of a new attack or an earlier strike, after authorities reported at 5:48 a.m. Kyiv time that a warehouse in the Sviatoshynskyi district had caught fire following a Russian attack.
According to the Ukrainian Air Force, Russia launched 80 strike UAVs against Ukraine from 6 p.m. on Sept. 15, including Shahed-type drones, their jet-powered variants, Gerbera drones and Parodiya decoys.
The attack was repelled by Ukrainian aviation, anti-aircraft missile units, electronic warfare and unmanned systems units, and mobile fire groups.
German Drone Maker Goes Underground Amid Suspected Russia Threat
Preliminary data showed that, as of 8 a.m., Ukrainian air defenses had shot down or suppressed 63 Russian UAVs. However, Russian strikes hit seven locations, while debris from intercepted targets fell at two other sites.
Previous attack on passenger train near Polish border
The attack came three days after Russian forces used a drone to target a passenger train near the Yahodyn border crossing in the Volyn region, about two kilometers (about 1.2 miles) from the Polish border.
The train was traveling from Kyiv to Warsaw. Passengers were evacuated after the attack, and no casualties were reported.
The incident also prompted the evacuation of European politicians traveling from Ukraine, including former British Prime Minister Boris Johnson, security advisers from European governments, members of the German Bundestag, diplomats and academics. The train had been stopped as a precaution.
Ukrzaliznytsia later clarified that the diplomatic train had been at Yahodyn station shortly before the locomotive was struck.
Former CIA Director David Petraeus was also on another train at the station at the time of the attack.
The company did not rule out the possibility that the jet-powered drone had targeted the diplomatic train, which had departed the station earlier after the UAV threat was detected.

articles.title: New photos reveal extensive damage to US bases from Iranian missile and drone strikes
articles.body:
New images obtained by CBS News reveal extensive damage to U.S. military aircraft, vehicles and buildings following Iranian missile and drone strikes on American bases across the Middle East.
The photographs were provided to the network by active-duty U.S. service members who asked to remain anonymous. “This is major damage to our bases that hasn’t been communicated to the American public,” one deployed service member told CBS News. “We’re standing there with our eyes closed getting punched in the face.”
The images document damage from Iranian missile and drone attacks at several U.S. positions in the region.
One of the most striking photographs was taken at Prince Sultan Air Base in Saudi Arabia. It shows a direct hit on the rear section of a U.S. Air Force Boeing E-3 Sentry, a four-engine airborne warning and control aircraft.
The aircraft’s tail is separated from its charred fuselage. The E-3, distinguished by the large rotating radar dome above its fuselage, is used for airborne surveillance, command and control and monitoring activity across large areas of airspace.
Other photographs from Prince Sultan show heavily damaged buildings and troop living quarters.
Some of the damaged structures stand alongside concrete barriers known as T-walls that appear to have remained intact. Such barriers have long been used to provide protection against threats including mortar fire and explosions, but the images underscore their limitations against aerial attacks involving missiles and drones.
Additional images were taken at Camp Buehring in Kuwait, a major staging area for U.S. Army ground forces in the Middle East.
There, photographs show damage to several armored vehicles as well as military aircraft and other equipment.
The new photographs add a visual dimension to the scale of losses described this week in the first inspector general report to Congress on the U.S. conflict with Iran.
According to the report cited by CBS, equipment losses were valued at as much as $3.7 billion and included nearly 60 aircraft. The report said U.S. Central Command recorded Iranian attacks against American bases in Kuwait, Bahrain, Qatar, the United Arab Emirates, Saudi Arabia, Iraq, Oman and Jordan.
The figures cover broader equipment losses connected to the conflict and should not be read as a valuation of the damage shown in the newly released photographs alone.
CBS has also reported damage to U.S. aircraft at other bases during the fighting. At Muwaffaq Salti Air Base in Jordan, for example, sources told the network that an A-10 Thunderbolt lost a wing in an Iranian strike while roughly eight F-15 fighter jets sustained lighter damage and were returned to service.
For the service member who spoke to CBS, however, the newly released photographs point to a broader concern about the vulnerability of U.S. positions in the region.
“These are not ‘squirters’ getting through,” the service member said, referring to terminology previously used for isolated incoming threats that penetrate defenses. “We’re not defending these bases. We’re just watching them get destroyed.”

articles.title: Iranian strikes caused widespread damage to US bases across Middle East: Report
articles.body:
Busra Nur Cakmak
16 September 2026•Update: 16 September 2026
Iranian missile and drone attacks caused widespread damage to US military positions across the Middle East, including buildings, vehicles and aircraft, according to newly obtained photographs reported by CBS News on Tuesday.
The images, provided to CBS News by active-duty service members on condition of anonymity because of military media restrictions, show damage at several US positions in the region.
“This is major damage to our bases that hasn't been communicated to the American public,” one deployed service member told the network. “We're standing there with our eyes closed getting punched in the face.”
At Prince Sultan Air Base in Saudi Arabia, one photograph shows what CBS News described as a direct hit on the rear section of a Boeing E-3 Sentry aircraft, with its tail severed from its charred fuselage.
Other images from the base show heavily damaged buildings and barracks alongside concrete “T-wall” barriers, which are designed primarily to provide protection against threats such as grenades and mortar fire.
Photos from Camp Buehring in Kuwait, a major staging area for US Army personnel, armored vehicles and some aircraft, also showed extensive damage, according to the report.
The images emerged as the US Defense Department's inspector general released a report estimating equipment losses from the Iran war at up to $3.7 billion, including nearly 60 aircraft.
In a mandatory report to Congress, the inspector general said US Central Command reported Iranian strikes on US bases in Kuwait, Bahrain, Qatar, the United Arab Emirates, Saudi Arabia, Iraq, Oman and Jordan.
The Pentagon did not respond to CBS News' request for comment.
“These are not ‘squirters’ getting through,” the service member said, referring to terminology used by Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth following a March 1 attack on Kuwait's Port of Shuaiba that killed six US troops.
“We're not defending these bases. We're just watching them get destroyed,” the service member added.

articles.title: Russia Rewards Captain Who Fired Flares at Danish Helicopter
articles.body:
Russian Defense Minister Andrei Belousov awarded the commander of a Russian corvette on Wednesday, Sept. 16, after the commander’s ship fired signal flares toward a Danish military helicopter over the Baltic Sea.
According to a statement from the Russian Defense Ministry, the unnamed commander of the Baltic Fleet corvette Soobrazitelny received the medal “For Combat Distinction,” for what Moscow described as “skillful and decisive actions” during the incident.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
The encounter took place at 2:22 p.m. on Monday, Sept. 14, while the Russian vessel was operating in international waters in the southwestern Baltic Sea, the ministry said.
Russia claimed that the Danish Air Force Fennec helicopter approached the corvette and did not respond to calls on an international communications channel.
“To prevent a provocation by the Danish helicopter, the corvette commander decided to launch two red signal flares,” the ministry said.
The helicopter subsequently left the area, according to Moscow’s account.
Denmark says flare narrowly missed helicopter
Denmark gave a sharply different description of the encounter, saying its helicopter was conducting routine photographic surveillance of the Russian vessel in international waters near the island of Gedser.
The Russian ship fired two flares toward the aircraft, with one passing close to it, the Danish Armed Forces said.
Danish Defense Minister Jeppe Bruus described the Russian vessel’s conduct as “very unprofessional seamanship,” saying other methods were available if its crew wanted to establish contact.
Russia Must List Protected Sites for Energy Truce
Denmark summoned Russian Ambassador Vladimir Barbin over the incident, which Foreign Minister Lars Løkke Rasmussen called “completely unacceptable.”
Danish Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen said the confrontation was part of a broader pattern of increasingly aggressive Russian conduct against Europe and NATO.
“Russia wants to intimidate and sow discord,” Frederiksen said, calling for European countries to strengthen their collective defense.
No injuries or damage to the Danish helicopter were reported.
Moscow blames Danish aircraft
Russia rejected Copenhagen’s account and accused the Danish helicopter crew of conducting dangerous maneuvers near the corvette.
Barbin delivered a diplomatic note to Denmark and demanded measures to prevent similar encounters, according to Reuters.
The ambassador also cited an alleged August 2025 incident involving a Danish helicopter and the Russian anti-submarine ship Vice-Admiral Kulakov. He claimed the aircraft flew at low altitude over the vessel without establishing radio contact.
Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said he did not have sufficient information to comment on the latest encounter.
The Soobrazitelny is a Project 20380 multipurpose corvette equipped with a 100-millimeter naval gun, air defense systems, and anti-ship missiles. It can also carry a Ka-27 anti-submarine helicopter.
Belousov’s decision to award its commander came two days after an encounter Denmark characterized as dangerous, amid growing concerns over Russian military activity around NATO’s Baltic members.

articles.title: Pentagon accuses Iran of trying to steal naval spy drone
articles.body:
Pentagon accuses Iran of trying to steal naval spy drone
The US military says it has attacked two boats that Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) allegedly used in an attempt to seize an American drone.
Iranian media previously reported that several fishermen were missing following a US attack off the coast of the southern port city of Kargan and near Larak Island.
Axios first reported the Pentagon’s account of the incident on Tuesday. US Central Command (CENTCOM) spokesperson Capt. Tim Hawkins confirmed the attempted seizure to the outlet and several others, saying the targeted unmanned surface vessel “remains under US operational control.”
The Associated Press said Hawkins identified the platform as an 8-meter Saildrone. California-based Saildrone produces several models of autonomous craft featuring a distinctive sail-like structure that carries solar panels and instruments, including a 7-meter model known as the Explorer.
The US Navy has used Saildrone products for intelligence gathering in the Middle East since at least 2021 and accused Iran of “stealing” some of the drones in 2022.
Earlier this month, the IRGC reported destroying a Saildrone Explorer and released footage showing the drone on fire.
The paramilitary force also published footage of what it described as “one of the most modern, unmanned, and smart submarines” operated by the US Navy that had been seized by Iran. CENTCOM said the submersible drone was an older model and did not carry sensitive equipment.
Tehran has previously reverse-engineered American military technology in an effort to bolster its own capabilities. Iran’s Shahed 171 Simorgh and Shahed Saeqeh drones resemble the US RQ-170, one of which Iran captured after it crossed into Iranian airspace on a surveillance mission in 2011.
Iranian kamikaze drones have played a significant role in the ongoing conflict with the US, which Washington launched alongside Israel in late February.
The continuing confrontation has significantly disrupted global energy markets, as both the US and Iran have sought to pressure the other through restrictions on oil exports from the Persian Gulf.

articles.title: Von der Leyen fleshes out Carney’s vision to paint Europe as leader of world’s middle powers
articles.body:
BRUSSELS ― Ursula von der Leyen used a major speech on Wednesday to pitch Europe as the leader of a group of like-minded countries that want to hold their own against rival powers such as Russia and China.
Not invited to join this EU-led coalition? Donald Trump’s United States.
Speaking before an audience that included Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney, who has publicly fallen out with Trump, the European Commission president spelled out her vision of Europe as a geopolitical leader with plans for new partnerships and closer relationships — the most notable of which was offering to explore possible “associate EU membership” status for Canada, in what would amount to a major first for the EU.
Advertisement
“In this new world, we must urgently reimagine our partnerships,” von der Leyen said in the speech at the European Parliament building in Strasbourg. She added that the EU wanted to “build global coalitions for our resilience and democracies. And here too only Europe ― with its size and power ― can take the lead.”
For the head of the EU’s executive branch, who’s now two years into her second five-year term, the speech amounted to a declaration of geopolitical legacy.
Coming one year after she declared Europe’s “independence moment” from the same platform, von der Leyen expanded on that idea in a speech that seemed to echo Carney’s own address at the World Economic Forum in Davos, Switzerland, in which he called for the world’s “middle powers” to stand together against autocrats.
In addition to offering Canada associate member status, von der Leyen suggested bringing the leaders of the U.K., Norway, Canada and Ukraine together in a newfangled “European Security Council” that would exist outside of NATO, offering a platform to discuss hybrid threats without the United States.
She also proposed that, with Europe in the role of coordinator, like-minded countries could jointly address challenges ranging from climate change to Chinese industrial overcapacity to the risks of frontier AI models.
“This speech was all about the big threats occupying European leaders: Russia and China, and to a lesser extent the United States,” said Mujtaba Rahman, Europe director at the Eurasia Group political consultancy. “It was all about how the EU can organize itself amid an imperialist Russia, a withdrawing America and a materialist China — it’s an attempt to draw those dots together.”
Advertisement
Yet for many of those watching, the speech was heavy on lofty ideas like associate membership for Canada — which faces considerable obstacles to become a reality — and light on practical new proposals to deal with Europe’s immediate challenges.
“Dr. von der Leyen is at her best when she diagnoses the ills of our time and of our Europe,” said French centrist lawmaker Nathalie Loiseau, who sits on the European Parliament’s security and defense committee. “We’re still waiting for the prescription that will help Europe regain its health.”
Skating over the issues
At a time when the EU economy is struggling with anemic growth and high inflation linked to runaway energy prices, the Commission president reiterated previously announced policy proposals on the economy, rather than pitching new ideas.
For example, the speech did not address how to meet Ukraine’s immediate financing needs — a pressing concern at a time when Kyiv has said it needs an additional €23 billion before the end of the year and the EU is its main financial benefactor.
It also included tough language on trade imbalances with China and the toll they are taking on Europe’s economy, but included no new policy proposal aside from doubling down on ongoing dialogue with Beijing.
It also skated over some of the major foreign policy issues dividing EU capitals, namely the Middle East and Israel’s relationship with the Palestinian territories in the West Bank and Gaza.
Advertisement
Von der Leyen made headlines last year by proposing to suspend the EU’s Association Agreement with Israel over humanitarian violations in Gaza. But this time she disappointed lawmakers who’d hoped she might offer a ban on trade with illegal Israeli settlements, an implicit recognition that her proposal from last year had floundered amid divisions between capitals.
Instead, she lamented the situation in Israel’s illegal West Bank settlements — and urged governments to overcome their disagreements.
Most of all, however, it was von der Leyen’s implicit suggestion that the EU should forge on without relying on the U.S., striking up new partnerships and setting up its own Security Council — outside of NATO — that seemed to unnerve some of the diplomats, lawmakers and officials watching her speech.
“I think it is a very bad idea. I think that it gives the signal to the world that NATO is irrelevant and we need to replace it with something,” said Riho Terras, an Estonian member of the conservative European People’s Party and former commander of his country’s armed forces. “Putin is talking about recreating the security infrastructure in Europe and now the European Union starts to do it itself by attacking NATO.”
The Security Council was “a dead-born idea,” said Željana Zovko, vice-chair of von der Leyen’s EPP.
Indeed, many watchers pointed to the reality that in areas ranging from technology to pharmaceuticals to defense procurement, the EU remains heavily dependent on the U.S.
“So much of what we need for Europe’s defense and our economy is done with the United States,” said a diplomat from an eastern EU country who was granted anonymity. “Why alienate them?”

articles.title: Zaporizhzhia Nuclear Plant Faces Falling Water Levels, Blackout Risk, Ukraine Says
articles.body:
Falling water levels and repeated losses of external electricity are creating an increasingly difficult safety situation at the Russian-occupied Zaporizhzhia Nuclear Power Plant, Ukraine’s military intelligence agency said.
None of the plant’s six reactors is generating electricity, and all remain in cold shutdown, the Military Intelligence of Ukraine (HUR) said in a statement.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
HUR said a work shift of about 1,150 employees, described as the minimum staffing level, was maintaining the facility’s safety systems.
The agency said the water level in the plant’s cooling pond had fallen from 12.86 meters in July to 12.63 meters in early August and 12.55 meters by the end of the month. It said the level was continuing to decline, while at least 15 meters was required for the facility’s normal operation.
The plant lost external electricity three times in August, on Aug. 1, 4 and 8, because of problems with the Ferrosplavna-1 power line, according to the intelligence agency.
HUR said the facility had experienced between 23 and 25 external power outages since Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022.
Backup diesel generators were activated during the August outages. However, their operation placed additional pressure on fuel supplies in the occupied region, the agency said.
“In the event of a prolonged total blackout, the plant would require about 150 metric tons of diesel fuel per day,” HUR said.
Ukrainian Businesses Expect Hryvnia Revenue Growth, Brace for War Through 2027
Nuclear plants depend on a continuous electricity supply to operate cooling and other essential safety systems even when their reactors are shut down.
Backup generators are intended to provide temporary power only if external supplies are lost.
Russian forces also disconnected internet access at the plant on Aug. 13 and 14, disrupting communications, the monitoring of key indicators and international oversight, HUR said.
The Zaporizhzhia plant, Europe’s largest nuclear power station, has been under Russian control since the early months of the full-scale invasion. The facility is located near the occupied city of Enerhodar in southeastern Ukraine.
HUR said residents of Enerhodar were experiencing repeated disruptions to electricity, water supplies and communications, as well as severe shortages of food and fuel.
The agency accused Russian forces of deliberately isolating the city’s information environment and mistreating civilians.
HUR also alleged that Moscow was seeking to incorporate the nuclear plant into Russia’s regulatory system by involving inspectors from Rostekhnadzor, the Russian agency responsible for technical and nuclear oversight.
It further accused Russia of using its representatives at the International Atomic Energy Agency to help legitimize the occupation. The intelligence agency cited a visit to the plant by IAEA Director General Rafael Grossi on Sept. 4, shortly before the agency’s General Conference in Vienna.
HUR claimed that Mikhail Chudakov, a Russian deputy director general at the IAEA, had secured changes to the agency’s Power Reactor Information System that displayed occupied Crimea as part of Russia and rendered the names of Ukrainian nuclear plants in Russian.
The intelligence agency also said Russian forces continued to use the Zaporizhzhia plant as a military base and shelter for occupation troops.
Russia has controlled the plant since March 2022, but Ukraine and the international community continue to recognize it as Ukrainian territory.

articles.title: Von der Leyen risks fresh EU-NATO turf war
articles.body:
BRUSSELS — European Commission chief Ursula von der Leyen on Wednesday proposed the EU take on a stronger role in security and tackling hybrid threats, reigniting a long-running turf battle with NATO over Europe's defense.
Speaking at her annual policy address in Strasbourg, von der Leyen pitched a new leaders’ crisis decision-making forum together with Canada, Norway, Ukraine and the U.K. She also floated a new urgent consultation procedure for hybrid attacks modeled on NATO’s Article 4.
“Our systems were made for a different world — they are driven by well-intentioned attempts at consensus and compromise,” she said. “But we need to consider whether they are still fit for purpose.”
The pitch is already stirring unease within NATO, which has bristled at any attempt by the EU to tackle military-adjacent threats and has warned against “unnecessary duplication.”
“I have seen many initiatives at the EU level during the recent years — none of them yet are really protecting member states,” said one senior NATO diplomat, who was granted anonymity to speak freely. “Of course, any initiative has to be assessed on its merits, but I do feel that NATO has delivered much more in concrete terms for collective security.”
The EU proposals underscore a growing sense that Europe is failing to deal with proliferating airspace violations, cyberattacks and sabotage attempts amid tensions over Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine.
“Cyberattacks and sabotage, arson and drone incursions. They are ramping up every day. So, as the threat level climbs, so must Europe's preparedness,” von der Leyen said.
The security council is supposed to help the EU react more decisively. NATO itself has struggled with how to respond to Russian provocations below the threshold of direct military attack.
Advertisement
The last time Article 4 was invoked — a formal request to consult allies due to a security threat — was by Estonia last year after three Russian fighter jets violated the country's airspace. No other capital has invoked it since.
Duplication drama
There are few details on von der Leyen’s ideas. Earlier European security council proposals — which the EU has rejected — include the idea of capitals delegating some defense decision-making powers to a smaller group of leaders in a crisis.
An Emergency Security Protocol, meanwhile, would allow one capital to convene all fellow EU members in a crisis “to coordinate a European response, to deter further escalation and to mitigate the impact,” von der Leyen said — almost identical to NATO’s Article 4 procedure.
In theory, a security council could help in “coordinating quick action” between the EU, NATO and other partners in a crisis that is “flexible across institutions,” said Giuseppe Spatafora, an analyst at the EU Institute for Security Studies. The emergency protocol, meanwhile, could protect non-NATO countries like Ireland, he said.
But the alliance insists it should take the lead on security. “NATO is the bedrock of our collective defence and we will continue to work closely with the EU in pursuit of our shared agenda,” said a NATO official speaking on behalf of the alliance.
Not all NATO allies are skeptical. On hybrid attacks, the “EU is better placed to put in place a mechanism to react, because it has more diverse tools than NATO,” said a second senior NATO diplomat.
Advertisement
EU Defense Commissioner Andrius Kubilius said von der Leyen's schemes were not intended to replace NATO.
“In order for Europeans to take primary responsibility for European defense, we need to have our own defense architecture,” he told POLITICO, “and we shall do that, not undermining NATO — keeping NATO structures as they are.”
But von der Leyen's ideas pose a risk of duplication, two NATO diplomats warned, adding that allies were not formally briefed by the EU on the proposals in advance.
Countries near Russia also fret that it could worsen their security situation. “It gives the signal to the world that NATO is irrelevant and we need to replace it with something,” said MEP Riho Terras, Estonia’s former chief of defense. “It is a very bad idea … which I hope will not have a future.”
The move also risks alienating some non-EU NATO members such as the U.S. and Turkey.
“The idea of a ‘European Security Union’ not including Türkiye, a major capable ally and a pillar of stability, security and peace at NATO’s southeastern flank, would be fatally flawed from the outset,” said one Turkish official.
Advertisement
The White House did not respond to a request for comment from POLITICO.
Setting up new EU bodies and holding consultations will not fix Europe’s underlying lack of political will to confront Russia and the need to match talk with action, said Oana Lungescu, a former longtime NATO official.
“Nations … should be talking about real capabilities and trying to harness real political will to impose costs on Russia,” she said. “How can you do that by focusing political energy and some resources ... towards yet another body?”
NATO’s “Article 4 works because it sits inside [its] Article 5” mutual defense clause, added a third NATO diplomat. “An EU ‘Article 4’ without an EU ‘Article 5’ is a consultation forum with a flattering name.”

articles.title: US charges five as alleged Kremlin assassination network reaches American soil
articles.body:
A US-based recruit was promised up to $1,500 to surveil a prominent Russian dissident before being offered $40,000 to “eliminate” or “disappear” the target, the US Justice Department (DOJ) said on 15 September.
The charges connect that alleged plot to what prosecutors describe as a wider Russian assassination network operating since at least 2024 against dissidents, defectors, and countries perceived as supporting Ukraine.
A federal grand jury in Manhattan indicted five alleged members of what prosecutors call the “RIS Network”:
- Yuri Khrameev, 63: A Russian national and former colonel in the Russian intelligence services who allegedly recruited people to kill Russian dissidents.
- Kirill Khrameev, 27: Yuri Khrameev’s son and an officer in the FSB, Russia’s principal security service and a successor to the Soviet KGB.
- Oemis Romagoza Durruthy, 35: A Cuban national living in Russia who allegedly coordinated attacks and arranged travel for operatives.
- Yaidel Delgado Suarez, 35: A Cuban national accused of recruiting people in the US for surveillance and murder.
- Angel Eduardo Castro, 22: A Venezuelan national accused of helping Suarez recruit US residents to spy on and kill a Russian dissident.
Suarez sent the US resident two locations associated with the dissident, according to the indictment. After the resident delivered photographs and videos, prosecutors say, Suarez and Castro made the $40,000 offer. When the resident declined to carry out the killing, they allegedly asked whether he knew “someone [who] can do the work.”
In 2025, the indictment alleges, Kirill Khrameev recruited a US citizen to photograph a target in Lithuania for a promised $200. Yuri Khrameev then offered approximately $25,000 to kill the man. When the recruit refused, Khrameev allegedly proposed a “simpler job”: burning a warehouse or attacking an electrical substation. He said the purpose was to target countries helping Ukraine, according to prosecutors.
Prosecutors also allege that Durruthy coordinated travel and logistics for attacks in Prague, Czechia, in June 2024 and in Lithuania that September. The Justice Department did not specify what either attack involved.
All five defendants are charged with conspiracy to finance terrorism, carrying up to 20 years in prison. Yuri Khrameev, Suarez, and Castro also face a murder-for-hire conspiracy charge carrying up to 10 years.
All five remain at large. Kremlin spokesperson Dmitry Peskov said Moscow saw no need to comment without “credible evidence,” Reuters reported. An indictment is an allegation, and the defendants are presumed innocent.
From military espionage to alleged murder plots
Since Russia’s full-scale invasion, its covert campaign against Ukraine’s Western allies has combined intelligence gathering with escalating sabotage. CSIS found that suspected Russian attacks in Europe nearly tripled from 2023 to 2024, often using locally recruited agents against infrastructure and industries supporting Ukraine.
In August 2025, US prosecutors charged active-duty soldier Taylor Adam Lee with trying to transmit Abrams tank information and deliver hardware to someone he believed represented the Russian government, allegedly in exchange for Russian citizenship. That case involved an American insider allegedly offering military secrets, not a proven Russian recruitment operation.

articles.title: Von der Leyen announces near-term aid measures for Ukraine
articles.body:
European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen has announced measures to assist Ukraine this winter, including providing unprecedented support, strengthening air defenses, and tightening sanctions against Russia.
“We know that the coming winter will be tough for Ukraine. But we also know that North Korean missiles and Russian drones cannot break the Ukrainian spirit of resistance. Because the people of Ukraine are fighting for something. They are fighting for the survival of their country, for their identity and for their freedom. And they are also fighting for our freedom and our self-determination. Our task remains to support Ukraine as best we can,” she stated in Strasbourg on Wednesday during the European Parliament's plenary session, as part of the annual 2026 State of the Union address.
She named providing assistance to Ukraine as “our strongest-ever support to Ukraine over the toughest winter of the war.” “Together with our partners, we will provide humanitarian aid and reinforce Ukraine's supplies of power and heating,” the President of the European Commission explained.
As a second point, von der Leyen highlighted the strengthening of Ukraine's air defense. “Last week, for the first time, we approved the purchase of American Patriot interceptor missiles. These now need to be delivered urgently. But we must also jointly reduce our dependence on a single supplier. That is why we would like to develop with Ukraine an affordable, modular missile-defence system. At the heart of this collaboration is the Freya project. Here we are combining the Ukrainians' combat experience and innovativeness with Europe's technological leadership. And, of course, our substantial production capacity. But Freya is only the beginning. More is needed,” she explained.
In this regard, von der Leyen announced the launch of a new program of joint projects with Ukrainian companies, utilizing remaining funds from the SAFE fund.
The European Commission President identified the tightening of sanctions against Russia as the third element of aid to Ukraine. “What is needed is not necessarily new sanctions, but above all the enforcement of existing sanctions,” she explained.

articles.title: Russian Drone Found on Polish Beach Carried Live Explosive Warhead, Prosecutors Confirm
articles.body:
- Category
- World
Russian Drone Found on Polish Beach Carried Live Explosive Warhead, Prosecutors Confirm
Polish military prosecutors told the Polish Press Agency (PAP) on September 16 that an armed Russian drone recovered from a beach at Rusinowo carried a live warhead, neutralized on site, and preliminarily identified as a Gerbera 2.
Col. Bartosz Okoniewski, deputy district prosecutor for military affairs at the District Prosecutor's Office in Poznań, informed the agency that the recovered aircraft had been armed.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
"It contained a fragmentation-high-explosive warhead together with a fuze," Okoniewski stated to PAP. "We managed to separate the warhead from the aircraft itself, and then, for safety reasons, the warhead was neutralized right there on the beach."
He added that the warhead was detonated on the evening of September 15. The airframe, now stripped of its warhead, was moved to a military site for detailed inspection, where preliminary findings indicated it was a Gerbera 2 type produced and used by Russia.
The drone was located on September 14 near Rusinowo, close to Jarosławiec, in Poland's West Pomeranian region. Deputy Prime Minister and Defense Minister Władysław Kosiniak-Kamysz announced the recovery that day, describing the object as a Russian military unmanned aircraft.
On September 16, Poland's Military Gendarmerie reported that soldiers had extracted, examined and neutralized components that could pose a threat, then secured the drone for laboratory analysis.
The on-site inspection, as Okoniewski detailed to PAP, was led by a prosecutor from the military division of the Szczecin-Niebuszewo District Prosecutor's Office. The Military Counterintelligence Service, military and police sappers, gendarmerie officers and the fire service also took part.
The prosecutor's office has opened a case under a preliminary classification of causing an event that threatens the life or health of many people, or property of great value, through an explosion. Investigators are additionally examining the use of an aircraft to cross the state border without the required permission.
The Gerbera is a cheap Russian drone typically fielded as a decoy and a reconnaissance platform alongside heavier Shahed-type strike aircraft, though armed and reconnaissance variants also exist.
Built largely from plywood and foam, the type carries a standard range of roughly 700 kilometers, with examples recovered abroad fitted with extra nose fuel tanks to stretch that reach.
Ukrainian estimates have put the production cost at around $10,000 per aircraft, enabling the drones to be launched in numbers that force defenders to expend far costlier interceptors.
According to PAP, Kosiniak-Kamysz linked the recovery to the downing of a Russian drone over Lithuania on the night of September 15. He suggested that the aircraft found in Poland might also have flown over Lithuania on September 13, where it was tracked and targeted for an attempted neutralization.
The drone then, in his account, "crossed the Lithuanian border with the Kaliningrad region and most likely operated over the Baltic." He indicated that Poland and Lithuania would investigate jointly, with the services of both countries cooperating.
The recovery followed a run of similar incidents across the Baltic in September. On September 13, an object that crossed from Lithuania into Russia's Kaliningrad region was identified as a drone.
Around the same time, a resident near Finland's Pellinki archipelago found an unmanned aircraft assessed as a Russian-made Geoscan 701. Two weeks earlier, on August 31, Polish fighter jets intercepted a Russian Il-20 reconnaissance aircraft over the Baltic Sea roughly 30 kilometers north of Łeba.

articles.title: A Russian drone strike destroyed a warehouse in Kyiv full of props from Volodymyr Zelensky’s former comedy studio, but the studio says all scheduled concerts will go ahead
articles.body:
A Russian drone strike destroyed a warehouse in Kyiv full of props from Volodymyr Zelensky’s former comedy studio, but the studio says all scheduled concerts will go ahead
An overnight Russian drone strike on Kyiv destroyed a warehouse storing props from the Kvartal 95 studio, the studio said.
The studio said the strike destroyed numerous sets, costumes, and other items used in Kvartal 95 concerts, television shows, films, and series over the past 20 years.
“Russian weapons can destroy property. But they cannot stop us. We will keep working, writing new jokes, and helping Ukraine’s defenders. All scheduled concerts will go ahead — with or without the props,” the studio said.
A warehouse belonging to the Olena Zelenska Foundation was also destroyed. The foundation said on social media that the warehouse burned to the ground but no one was hurt. It held humanitarian aid that the foundation had purchased or received from partners to distribute to children, families, and institutions across Ukraine.
Ukraine’s State Emergency Service said a Russian drone struck a warehouse in Kyiv’s Sviatoshynskyi district, sparking a fire and injuring one person.
Kvartal 95 is a Ukrainian studio that Volodymyr Zelensky co-founded and was part of before becoming president. The studio was established in 2003 out of the KVN comedy team 95-y Kvartal. For more than 20 years, it has produced television shows, films, series, and concert programs.
