articles.title: Russia demands using of russified place names for occupied Ukrainian territories in IAEA system – GUR
articles.body:
Russian representatives at the IAEA have succeeded in having Crimea designated as Russian territory within the IAEA’s global integrated information system (PRIS) and are demanding further Russification of the names of occupied Ukrainian settlements, according to the Main Intelligence Agency (GUR) of the Ministry of Defence of Ukraine.
"For instance, IAEA Deputy Director General Mikhail Chudakov—a Russian national—secured the agency's support for displaying the temporarily occupied territory of the Autonomous Republic of Crimea as part of the Russian Federation in the updated IAEA global integrated information system (PRIS)," the GUR stated in a Telegram post regarding the current situation at the Zaporizhia Nuclear Power Plant (ZNPP) on Wednesday.
It is also reported that Russian representatives within the organization are demanding the use of Russified names for Ukrainian settlements in the system, specifically: Chernobyl, Rovno, Khmelnitski, and Zaporozhye.
Furthermore, the GUR reports a danger posed by the continuous drop in water levels in the ZNPP cooling pond. While the level stood at 12.86 meters in July 2026, it fell to 12.63 meters in early August and to 12.55 meters by the end of the month, with the decline continuing. A level of 15 meters is considered the minimum required to meet the plant's operational needs.
It is also noted that instances of external power supply outages at the plant have become more frequent. In August, the ZNPP lost external power three times. Additionally, the plant is experiencing internet connectivity issues. On August 13–14, 2026, the network was disconnected due to the actions of Russian occupying forces, hindering communication, data monitoring, and international oversight. The Kremlin has also stepped up the implementation of its strategy to integrate the Zaporizhia Nuclear Power Plant (ZNPP) into its "legal framework"—specifically, the aggressor state's Federal Service for Environmental, Technological and Nuclear Supervision (Rostekhnadzor) has dispatched a special team of inspectors to the plant.
"At the same time, Moscow is seeking, through its representatives at the IAEA, to russify the organization and leverage the agency's international status to justify the occupation of the ZNPP. One of the objectives of this hybrid campaign is to 'normalize' the information landscape and pave the way for the further legitimization of Russian control over the Ukrainian nuclear power plant," the message notes. As part of these efforts, Russia attempted to orchestrate and exploit for its own ends a visit by IAEA Director General Rafael Grossi to the occupied ZNPP ahead of the 70th session of the IAEA General Conference in Vienna (September 14–17), where the issue of nuclear safety in Ukraine is set to be addressed. Grossi visited the ZNPP on September 4.

articles.title: Iran warns against growing use of AI in wars
articles.body:
Addressing UNESCO’s 2026 Global Forum on the Ethics of Artificial Intelligence (GFEAI 2026) in Riyadh on Wednesday, Hossein Simaee Sarraf stressed that technology is not neutral and warned that AI could be used as a means of oppression.
“Artificial intelligence does not act fairly by itself,” Simaee remarked, adding that algorithms can sometimes destroy more than they create and platforms can become sources of harm instead of development.
He also cautioned that even surveillance must have limits, noting that greater oversight of governments and those in power is desirable, but monitoring ordinary citizens’ behavior, relationships and intentions could create an “invisible dictatorship.”
“Today, data is being used in actions that violate human rights and even lead to the killing of children,” the minister noted, questioning whether AI platforms and technology developers should bear responsibility for how their systems are used.
Simaee pointed out that AI can also be used “to identify and precisely target human beings with missiles,” raising serious ethical questions over its military applications.
Referring to the attack on a school in southern Iran by the US using AI, which resulted in the martyrdom of 168 students and teachers, Simaee highlighted that the issue required deep consideration and urgent solutions.
The minister further cautioned that AI could widen existing inequalities, noting that an ethical framework should not only prevent harm but also guarantee equal access to the technology.
“Technology must serve humanity, and artificial intelligence must expand human freedom, rather than restrict it,” Simaee stressed, calling on developing countries to build AI systems suited to their own languages and cultures.
According to Press TV, his warnings come as AI-assisted warfare has increasingly featured in Tel Aviv and Washington’s military operations.
Investigations suggest that Israel has extensively used digital tools Lavender and the Gospel to identify and target Palestinians in Gaza, where the regime has killed more than 73,000 people and wounded 173,000 others.
Reports have also linked AI-assisted surveillance and targeting technologies to the regime’s military aggression in Lebanon, where its forces have killed 4,383 people and wounded 12,406 others.
Furthermore, during the US-Israeli aggression against Iran, several AI platforms developed by major technology companies, including Microsoft, Apple and Amazon, were combined with satellite imagery, radar, drone and communications data to create a battlefield picture and support targeting decisions.
He underscored that the region’s most important priority is now an end to unilateral coercive measures and the establishment of peace, describing sanctions as “unethical” and peace and security as an ethical necessity.
Simaee also noted that Iran enjoys capable universities, researchers, knowledge-based companies and specialized institutions, stressing that these capacities should be brought together through greater cooperation, data sharing and joint use of infrastructure.
MNA

articles.title: US opts not to back Saudi Arabia in Yemen after meeting Houthi leaders
articles.body:
Officials from the US met Houthi leaders over the weekend at the country’s embassy in Muscat, Oman, it has been confirmed, leading to the US decision not to intervene to help Saudi Arabia drive back a Houthi advance inside Yemen.
The Iran-backed militant group reassured the US that the ceasefire agreement between the two sides struck in 2025 still held and the movement had no intention of attacking US shipping in the Red Sea. Only Saudi-linked shipping was regarded as a target owing to its blockade of Yemen, the Houthis confirmed.
The meeting helps to explain Donald Trump’s decision to condemn the Houthi advance down the west coast of Yemen for threatening freedom of navigation through the Bab al-Mandab strait, but so far to reject any military response in support of Riyadh. The US is already embroiled in an expensive and resource sapping conflict with Iran, which backs the Houthis.
The US labelled the Houthis as a foreign terrorist entity in March 2025, but in the recent past American officials have met leaders from Hamas, Hezbollah and Iran. The US vice-president, JD Vance, confirmed on Monday that the US was in direct contact with the Houthis.
The US refusal to become directly involved has put pressure on Saudi Arabia to reach either a diplomatic solution with the Houthis over the future governance of Yemen, or to try to build a regional alliance with Pakistan and Turkey to force the Houthis back. In a lightning offensive last week, the Houthis seized control of large swathes of western Yemen along the Red Sea coast.
A former deputy US ambassador to Yemen, Nabeel Khoury, said a “kind of tacit understanding” had been struck between the Trump administration and the Houthis. Khoury added: “The Houthis are promising the American administration that American and international navigation will not be affected in the Red Sea, but the only danger is to Saudi ships or those carrying Saudi oil.”
In an attempt to build popular support against the Houthis in the region, Riyadh made the disputed claim that the Houthis had fired a drone at the holy city of Mecca on Tuesday, but the missile had been destroyed by Saudi defence forces. It said the drone was entering a prohibited airspace close to Mecca’s most holy shrines. The drone was intercepted at about 6.50pm local time on Tuesday, according to coalition spokesperson Maj Gen Turki al-Maliki.
Saudi Arabia said any attack on Mecca was a red line and the move was condemned in lengthy statements by the UN-recognised Yemen government based in Aden as well as the 57-country Organisation of Islamic Cooperation. The Pakistani prime minister, Shehbaz Sharif, condemned what he described as a “dastardly and heinous” attempted attack on Mecca. “The people of Pakistan are saddened and perturbed by this outrageous act,” he said in a statement posted on X.
The Houthi leadership – followers of a Shia Zaydism that respects the pilgrimage to Mecca – dismissed the claim as the lie of the century, and said such worn-out lies had been used before and fooled no one.
The Houthi’s deputy foreign minister, Abdul Wahid abu Ras, said “whoever opened the land of the two holy mosques to debauchery and entertainment parties, and whoever defiled the land of the two holy mosques by the presence of Zionist Jews in it, is the one who targets Mecca, Medina and the Islamic holy sites”.
The Houthis countered that they had shot down a Saudi F-15 plane close to Marib, and attacked an Aramco plant in the Red Sea port city of Yanbu. No supporting evidence was provided by the Houthi military spokesperson, but the head of the Houthi negotiating team, Mohammed abdul Salam, said the downing of the plane was a warning to the west not to fall victim to Saudi propaganda.
Mohammed al-Farah, a Houthi political bureau member, said: “The truth is that Saudi Arabia is experiencing a real predicament in Yemen. It became embroiled in a war, a siege and an occupation, and then failed to achieve its goals.
“Today, it is looking for external solutions, so it is begging the international community, warning the world about Bab al-Mandab and requesting support from Pakistan, Turkey, America, Israel and Egypt. Then it is trying to mobilise Muslims with a false pretext called ‘targeting Mecca’.”
Separately, Israeli officials have leaked details of a secret meeting between military commanders from the US, Israel and several Arab states in Germany last week to discuss the war launched by Israel and the US against Iran. The report from the Axios journalist Barak Ravid said the “private retreat” was organised by the head of US Central Command, Adm Brad Cooper.
Citing two unnamed Israeli officials, Ravid reported that the meeting was attended by the military chiefs of staff of Israel, Saudi Arabia, the United Arab Emirates, Bahrain, Kuwait, Qatar, Jordan and Egypt. It was the first such gathering since the US and Israel went to war with Iran more than six months ago. Israel, once a target for the Houthis, is offering to intervene in Yemen on Saudi Arabia’s behalf.
A meeting of the UN security council on Tuesday condemned any attempt to close the Red Sea, but the meeting was notable for the Russian envoy beginning to edge away from its previous stance that the UN-recognised government based in Aden was the only legitimate government inside the country.
In Beijing, the Iranian foreign minister, Abbas Araghchi, on Wednesday met his Chinese counterpart, Wang Yi, in an effort to secure support for its plans for the future administration of the strait of Hormuz. The strait remains closed owing to separate Iranian and US blockades.
A Chinese foreign ministry spokesperson said China did not want to see further regional tension spill over into Yemen and the Red Sea. The Chinese called on the US to return to the talks based on the memorandum of understanding agreed between the two sides in June. Beijing, the main importer of Iranian oil, is eager for a settlement and is resisting any suggestion that US secondary sanctions applied to countries trading with Iran should apply to its own country.
Oil prices remain well over $100 (£74) a barrel and a key Saudi east-west pipeline remains closed because of a bombing incident.

articles.title: Zelensky Says Putin Wants All of Ukraine, Rejects ‘Win-Win’ Peace Concept
articles.body:
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky said Russian President Vladimir Putin’s goal in the war extends far beyond seizing additional Ukrainian territory, adding that Moscow ultimately wants Ukraine to become part of Russia.
Speaking to CBC News in an interview, he said Ukraine could accept a ceasefire along the current line of contact if Russia agreed to halt fighting without conditions and the conflict then moved to diplomacy.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
“We are ready for this,” Zelensky said, referring to a potential halt in fighting along the existing front line.
He said negotiations could then continue with the mediation of international partners, adding that a ceasefire without conditions would be preferable to continued fighting.
Zelensky rejects ‘win-win’ concept
Zelensky also rejected the idea that there could be a “win-win” outcome for Russia and Ukraine after the losses caused by the war.
“There is no win-win in this war,” he said, adding that the war ceased to be a situation in which both sides could benefit from the moment it began and caused human casualties.
Zelensky added the most important victory would be to end the war and protect human lives, rather than for either Ukraine or Russia to claim victory.
He acknowledged that he and US presidential envoy Jared Kushner had somewhat different views on the issue but said he was encouraged that Kushner and fellow envoy Steve Witkoff had traveled to Kyiv after multiple visits to Moscow.
ISW Russian Offensive Campaign Assessment, September 15, 2026
Zelensky said the envoys had asked Ukrainian officials not to publicly discuss some of their proposals while the two sides examined them in greater detail. He added that Ukraine was preparing for a meeting with US President Donald Trump in New York expected later in September.
‘He needs Ukraine’
The Ukrainian president pushed back against the idea that Putin could be satisfied by obtaining a specific portion of Ukrainian territory.
Asked about Kushner’s comments that territory remained a key sticking point and that Putin had outlined the territorial line he wanted, Zelensky said the issue was not simply about “some kilometers” of land.
“The problem is that we have to change Putin’s mind,” Zelensky said.
He argued that it made little sense to suggest Putin needed only a particular part of Ukraine, given that Russia already controls vast territory elsewhere.
“He needs Ukraine,” Zelensky said. “He needs Ukraine [to] be a part of Russia.”
Zelensky said this was why Ukraine could not simply accept a territorial concession as the basis for a lasting settlement.
He also addressed the prospect of meeting Putin directly, saying he was willing to sit across from his adversary if doing so could bring the parties closer to peace.
He acknowledged that such a meeting was not something he personally wanted, saying he would rather spend the time with his family.
“But he is an enemy, of course,” Zelensky said.
Zelensky said he would nevertheless meet Putin if negotiations could produce meaningful progress toward peace. He argued that he understood Putin’s objective and believed the Russian leader would continue trying to occupy Ukraine unless Ukraine remained strong and received credible security guarantees.
“He will not change his goal,” Zelensky said.
For Ukraine, he added, security guarantees would need to ensure that Russia could not simply resume its attempt to occupy the country after a ceasefire or peace agreement.

articles.title: Russian attacks across Ukraine kill at least 9, injure 36 as drone strike on bus kills 5
articles.body:
Russian attacks across Ukraine kill at least 9, injure 36 as drone strike on bus kills 5
At least nine people were killed and 36 others injured in Russian attacks across Ukraine over the past day, including five people killed when a Russian drone struck a passenger bus in Dnipropetrovsk Oblast, local authorities said on Sept. 16.
A Russian drone struck a passenger bus in the Nikopol district of Dnipropetrovsk Oblast on the morning of Sept. 16, killing five people at the scene and injuring at least seven others, local Governor Oleksandr Hanzha said.
"Almost every day, we see Russia striking civilian transport. People who were simply going about their business are killed and injured," Human Rights Ombudsman Dmytro Lubinets said.
In the morning, Preisdent Zelensky said, "Each of these strikes is about the lives of ordinary people who need to be protected by forcing Russia to stop its stupid war."
The morning attack followed another wave of Russian strikes on Dnipropetrovsk Oblast the previous evening. Two people were injured on Sept. 15 as Russian forces attacked three districts more than 10 times with drones, artillery, and aerial bombs, Hanzha added.
Russian forces launched 80 drones overnight, including Shahed-type attack drones, jet-powered variants, Gerbera drones, and decoy drones, the Air Force said. Ukrainian air defenses shot down 63 drones, while strikes were recorded at seven locations. Debris from downed drones fell at two locations, according to the Air Force.
In Zaporizhzhia Oblast, one person was killed and seven others were injured in Russian attacks on Zaporizhzhia and the surrounding district, Ivan Fedorov, co-chair of the Regional Defense Council, said. Russian forces launched 746 strikes against 52 settlements in the region over the past day, according to Fedorov.
In Kherson Oblast, Russian attacks killed one person and injured seven others, regional authorities said. Russian forces targeted critical infrastructure as well as residential areas, damaging three apartment buildings, agricultural machinery and vehicles.
In Donetsk Oblast, two people were killed in Sloviansk and one person was injured in the region over the past day, Governor Vadym Filashkin said.
In Kharkiv Oblast, Russian attacks injured 12 people over the past day, Governor Oleh Syniehubov said. Russian forces used 12 guided aerial bombs, a Geran-2 drone, a Molniya drone, and more than 100 drones of types that authorities were still working to identify, according to Syniehubov.
In Kyiv Oblast, Russian drone attacks damaged 17 sites over the past day and the morning of Sept. 16, with damage recorded in the Bila Tserkva, Boryspil, Brovary, Bucha, and Obukhiv districts, according to local authorities. A driver in the Obukhiv district suffered a concussion from the blast wave after a house, tractor, and vehicle were damaged.

articles.title: Moscow court frees four truck drivers unwittingly used by Ukraine in 2025 ‘Operation Spiderweb’ drone attack on Russian military airfields
articles.body:
Moscow court frees four truck drivers unwittingly used by Ukraine in 2025 ‘Operation Spiderweb’ drone attack on Russian military airfields
The Moscow City Court released four drivers whose trucks Ukrainian security services used to launch drones at Russian military airfields during Operation Spiderweb, Kommersant reported.
At a hearing on September 16, the court denied an Investigative Committee representative’s request to extend the detention of Andrey Merkuryev, Alexander Zaitsev, Mikhail Ryumin, and Sergey Kanurin. The four have been charged with carrying out a terrorist attack and transporting explosives as part of an organized group.
Investigators allege that the drivers belonged to a group established by Ukrainian-born Artem and Ekaterina Timofeyev, who were recruited by the Security Service of Ukraine to carry out terrorist attacks in Russia and have been placed on a wanted list. Some of the drivers worked for a business registered as a sole proprietorship in Artem Timofeyev’s name. The Investigative Committee alleges that he approached the others as an ordinary customer seeking transportation services.
The Investigative Committee completed its investigation and sent the case to the Prosecutor General’s Office, but First Deputy Prosecutor General Anatoly Razinkin declined to approve the indictment. According to Razinkin, investigators had found no direct evidence of the defendants’ guilt, and the circumstantial evidence was insufficient to bring the case to court. Investigators disagreed and appealed the decision. The Moscow City Court then denied the Investigative Committee’s request to extend the defendants’ detention and ordered their release.
On June 1, 2025, the Security Service of Ukraine carried out Operation Spiderweb, using drones to attack military airfields in four Russian regions. The drones were hidden inside wood-frame houses transported by five long-haul truck drivers. One driver, 62-year-old Vasily Pytikov, was killed in an explosion during the operation. It later emerged that authorities had arrested the other four truckers — Merkuryev, Zaitsev, Ryumin, and Kanurin. Ukrainian officials said the drivers were unaware of the drones hidden in their trucks.
The defendants deny any wrongdoing. They said they called law enforcement themselves after the drones flew out of their trucks and also tried to bring the drones down.

articles.title: Caine: US Must Prepare for Forces to Be ‘Tracked in Real Time’
articles.body:
NATIONAL HARBOR, Md.—Chairman of the Joint Chiefs Gen. Dan Caine said the U.S. needs to prepared for future conflicts in which its adversaries will be able to closely track the location of American forces and attack with autonomous systems that use artificial intelligence.
“We have to assume from now on that our formations will be hunted by autonomous systems, jammed across the spectrum and tracked in real time,” Caine said in a keynote address at AFA’s Air, Space & Cyber Conference on Sept. 16.
“And we have to transition the joint force to be prepared to fight and win our future wars by generating and delivering lethality at scale with an agile, optimized, high-low mix of combat capabilities,” he added.
The notion of an increasingly transparent battlefield in which U.S. forces will have few places to hide has been hammered home by the ongoing conflict with Iran. Tehran, the State Department said in May, has used satellite imagery provided by Chinese companies to strike at American forces in the Middle East.
Brig. Gen. Todd Benson, the commander of Space Forces Central, said at the conference that small nations and even subnational groups could also potentially access satellite imagery to track American forces.
“I’ve been coining the term hyper-transparent warfare,” Benson said in a Sept. 15 media roundtable. “Nothing you do today is without being seen. You just can’t hide anymore, and so that’s great for us for our advantage. But you have to assume that any adversary will find some way to access imagery, and so we have to use that, and we have to operate knowing that we can be seen.”
It was a theme Caine underscored as well.
“Future conflicts will demand that we operate without the assumptions of uncontested access, secure rare areas, or uninterrupted or uncontested sustainment,” Caine said. “In the future fight, advantage will go to the side who can see first, who can understand first, decide first, and act first, and along the way be a learning organization”
The chairman noted several ways the U.S. can prepare for future fights.
One way is exploit artificial intelligence and cyber capability, said Caine, who noted the use of AI to enable an unmanned vessel to rescue two U.S. soldiers after an Apache attack helicopter was downed in June near the coast of Oman.
“That capacity did not appear overnight,” said Caine. “What made this possible was a bunch of entrepreneurial Sailors and members of the joint force on watch floors at piers, managing networks of unmanned systems across thousands of miles of water and using AI to turn massive amounts of data into a crisp, clear, perfect maritime picture that allowed us to go grab those two Soldiers in the water.”
Caine said it is also important for commands to empower young Airmen and Guardians to innovate and take risks.
“I need you to be adaptive leaders. The fight will not wait for perfect requirements, perfect processes, or perfect information,” said Caine. “You must always be able to recognize when the old way is no longer sufficient, get close to the problem, and help build a better solution.”
He also stressed the important for industry and the government to cooperate more closely.
“We cannot expect industry to invest in capacity, manufacturing or top talent when we’re moving requirements around, but we have to be able to adapt more quickly. That means sharing risk across government and industry,” he added. “We can buy almost anything in life, but we cannot buy time.”

articles.title: Defying Mamdani, Netanyahu to visit NYC but not land at JFK
articles.body:
Breadcrumb
Defying Mamdani, Israel's Netanyahu to visit NYC but not land at JFK
Fearing possible arrest, Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s plane will not land at John F. Kennedy International Airport when he arrives in New York later this month, with the Israeli leader expected to travel under heightened security.
According to Israeli media reports, the decision not to land Netanyahu’s official aircraft, Wing of Zion, at JFK was driven by concerns that New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani could prevent the plane from remaining at the airport throughout Netanyahu’s visit. The arrangement had previously been granted to the leaders of Israel and Iran.
Netanyahu is scheduled to arrive in the United States on 23 September, address the UN General Assembly on the afternoon of 24 September and return to Israel that night, according to Israel’s UN envoy Danny Danon.
Netanyahu and other Israeli officials are wanted by the International Criminal Court over alleged war crimes and crimes against humanity in connection with Israel’s genocidal war on the Gaza Strip.
Neither the United States nor Israel is a party to the Rome Statute, and the Trump administration has imposed sanctions on ICC staffers in a campaign to dismantle the tribunal.
While New York City does not have the authority to enforce an ICC arrest warrant, Mamdani has said he would seek to have the federal government enforce such a warrant.
The visit is expected to involve unprecedented security measures, with the US Secret Service significantly increasing its role in Netanyahu’s protection. The agency is expected to accompany him from the moment he lands until his departure for Israel.
The visit is also expected to draw protests outside the hotel where Netanyahu will stay and outside the United Nations headquarters as he delivers his address.
At the same time, right-wing pro-Israel groups within New York’s Jewish community are organising rallies in his support.
Following the decision not to land Wing of Zion at JFK, Israeli authorities are reportedly exploring the possibility of landing the aircraft at Newark Liberty International Airport in New Jersey or at a nearby military base, allowing it to remain on the ground for the duration of Netanyahu’s visit.
Netanyahu is not expected to meet US President Donald Trump, who is reportedly scheduled to leave New York before the Israeli prime minister arrives.
Netanyahu’s UN speech comes amid Israel’s election campaign and is expected to be aimed in large part at an Israeli audience. He is expected to use the address to highlight his alleged wartime "achievements" and appeal to Israeli voters. The election is in late October.
Over the past three years, Israel has occupied parts of Gaza, Lebanon and Syria, fought two rounds of wars against Iran, and conducted strikes on Yemen, Qatar and other countries.

articles.title: Ukraine’s SBS Drones Hit 6,280 Russian Troops in 15 Days, Outpacing August Figures
articles.body:
- Category
- War in Ukraine
Ukraine’s SBS Drones Hit 6,280 Russian Troops in 15 Days, Outpacing August Figures
Ukraine’s Unmanned Systems Forces reported more than 6,000 confirmed strikes on Russian personnel during the first half of September, surpassing the figure recorded over the same period in August, commander Major Robert “Madyar” Brovdi said on September 16.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
According to Brovdi, Unmanned Systems Forces units killed or incapacitated 6,280 Russian troops during the first 15 days of September, compared with 4,998 over the corresponding period in August.
Brovdi said the largest share of the reported strikes on Russian personnel was recorded in the Dobropillia, Huliaipole, and Pokrovsk sectors. Ukrainian drone units reported 1,806 such strikes in the Dobropillia sector, 1,927 in the Huliaipole sector, and 617 near Pokrovsk.
If the current pace of Russian troop deployments continues and weather conditions remain favorable for drone operations, Brovdi said the monthly figure could reach around 12,500 by the end of September. By comparison, the Unmanned Systems Forces recorded 11,010 confirmed strikes on Russian personnel throughout August.
Brovdi also said Ukrainian drone units expect operations to intensify between October and December, citing anticipated Russian efforts to deploy additional personnel.
“We expect an intensification in October–December 2026 due to the enemy’s intention to deploy an additional 300,000 personnel, which would be exactly twice the previous monthly reinforcement levels,” Brovdi said.
His assessment comes as Russia continues to sustain substantial personnel losses in Ukraine. According to Ukraine’s General Staff, Russian forces recorded 301,030 personnel killed or wounded between the beginning of 2026 and September 15.
To illustrate the scale of the reported losses, the General Staff said the figure is equivalent to the personnel strength of nearly 150 motorized rifle regiments, based on an average of roughly 2,000 troops per brigade.
The heaviest losses were recorded during the summer, when 124,170 Russian troops were reported killed or wounded between June and August. The monthly toll stood at 39,290 in June, increased to 42,860 in July, and reached 42,020 in August.
The losses continued into September, with another 20,360 Russian personnel reported killed or wounded between the beginning of the month and September 15, according to the General Staff.
As Russian battlefield losses continue to mount, Moscow is seeking to expand its military ranks. Russia could mobilize as many as 600,000 additional personnel by the end of 2027 to replenish losses and sustain manpower levels for ongoing offensive operations in Ukraine.

articles.title: Ukraine proposes record defence spending next year as war costs soar
articles.body:
Ukraine proposes record defence spending next year as war costs soar
KYIV, Sept 16 - Ukraine is proposing record defence spending for 2027 as the cost of the war with Russia, now in its fifth year, rises and the country needs more financial support from its partners, officials said on Wednesday.
Defence spending is expected to hit 4.89 trillion hryvnias ($110 billion) in 2027, 12% higher than this year. It accounted for about two-thirds of the total spending in a draft 2027 budget of 7.27 trillion hryvnias presented to parliament on Wednesday.
Budget revenues are forecast at 5.6 trillion hryvnias.
"This is the sixth budget of the full-scale war, and it's again bigger than the previous one. During these years, the war has become more expensive," said Roksolana Pidlasa, head of the parliamentary budget committee told lawmakers.
"At the same time, state revenues ... are not growing at the same pace as spending is increasing."
The daily cost of the war has risen to $190 million this year compared with $116 million in 2022 at the start of Russia's invasion, Pidlasa said.
Finance Minister Sergii Marchenko said told parliament that Ukraine would require more than $52 billion in international financial aid next year.
President Volodymyr Zelenskiy's government has secured commitments from partners to cover around $20 billion and was in talks on how to cover the remaining amount, he said.
Marchenko said that Russian assets frozen by Ukraine's European allies could become a key source to cover the budget gap in 2027.
Lawmakers have until October 1 to review the draft budget and submit their proposals. The spending plan must be passed by parliament in three readings by December 1.
UKRAINE'S FINANCIAL SITUATION MORE COMPLICATED
Ukraine's financial situation was getting more complicated this year as Russia intensified its strikes on Ukrainian businesses and infrastructure, the finance minister said.
As the damages has grown, budget revenues have started falling, but at the same time the Ukrainian armed forces have required more funds, Marchenko said. Currently, Ukraine faces an unfunded additional gap for its defence spending of $27 billion this year as the country seeks to increase army wages and further increase its weapons production.
During the earlier years of the war, Ukraine covered its defence needs with its own revenues and relied on foreign financial aid to finance its social and humanitarian spending.
Since the start of the invasion, Ukraine has received about $198 billion in fiscal aid from its foreign partners with the EU providing the bulk.
But to ensure smooth financing from partners, Kyiv needs to push through tax and governance reforms, and meet a number of financial and budget requirements despite wartime challenges.
On Wednesday, parliament passed a bill to impose taxes on foreign parcels in the first reading, moving closer to satisfying one of the key conditions to unlock funds from the International Monetary Fund and the European Union.
"Parliament advanced two essential tax and customs reforms that bring Ukraine's e-commerce framework closer to EU standards, strengthen fiscal resilience and support fairer competition for Ukrainian businesses," Marchenko said.
"This progress also paves the way for around 4 billion euros in EU macro-financial support." REUTERS

articles.title: Russia sentences Ukrainian man to 8.5 years in prison in first known case under new ‘aiding the enemy’ law
articles.body:
Russia sentences Ukrainian man to 8.5 years in prison in first known case under new ‘aiding the enemy’ law
The Pskov Regional Court sentenced a Ukrainian citizen born in 1999 to eight years and six months in a maximum-security penal colony for “assisting the enemy in activities known to be directed against Russia’s security” under Article 276.1 of the Criminal Code, according to the court’s website.
Investigators alleged that the man sent money to foundations supporting the Ukrainian Armed Forces while living and working in Russia.
The court also fined him 500,000 rubles and ordered his cellphone forfeited to the state because it had been “used in the commission of the crime.”
The court did not name the defendant. Mediazona identified him as 26-year-old Anton Demidenko.
His arrest was first reported in July 2025, after Moscow’s Lefortovsky District Court ordered him held in custody. At the time, it was the first known use of Article 276.1, which criminalizes “assisting the enemy.”
Article 276.1 was added to the Criminal Code in late 2024. It applies to foreign nationals and stateless people who provide financial, advisory, or other assistance to “a foreign state or an international or foreign organization directly opposing Russia in an armed conflict, hostilities, or other actions involving weapons and military equipment.” The minimum sentence is 10 years in prison, meaning Demidenko received a sentence below the statutory minimum. The reason is unknown.

articles.title: Russians strike infrastructure facility in Poltava Oblast: warehouse catches fire
articles.body:
Russians strike infrastructure facility in Poltava Oblast: warehouse catches fire
Russian forces have struck an infrastructure facility in Poltava Oblast, causing a warehouse to catch fire.
Source: Vitalii Diakivnych, Head of Poltava Oblast Military Administration
Details: A Russian strike caused a fire at an infrastructure facility in the Poltava district.
"The fire engulfed a warehouse building. Early reports indicate that there are no injuries," Diakivnych said.
He warned that the fire could temporarily affect air quality in nearby areas due to smoke.
Residents are advised to keep their windows closed and limit time spent outdoors.
"Meanwhile, there is no direct threat to the lives and health of residents of nearby villages. The situation is under the control of emergency services," Diakivnych said.
He reported that a Russian drone struck the industrial facility. The region's energy infrastructure also came under attack.
"According to unofficial monitoring channels, enemy strike drones were detected flying over the Poltava district at approximately 02:30-03:40. The air-raid warning in the oblast was in effect for several hours," local media outlet Poltavshchyna reported.
Background: A power line was damaged by debris from Russian aerial assets, leaving 18 settlements in Mykolaiv Oblast without electricity.

articles.title: Ukrainian forces strike Russian bomber in Crimea and drone ground control stations in Donetsk Oblast
articles.body:
Ukrainian forces strike Russian bomber in Crimea and drone ground control stations in Donetsk Oblast
Ukraine's defence forces struck a Russian Su-24 tactical bomber in Saky in temporarily occupied Crimea and a number of other important Russian military assets on 15 September and on the night of 15-16 September.
Source: Ukraine's General Staff
Details: The Ukrainian military reported that a Su-24 aircraft had been hit at the Saky airfield in temporarily occupied Crimea. The extent of the damage is still being assessed.
A site used by Russian forces to store, prepare and launch attack UAVs was also struck near the city of Donetsk.
Russian UAV ground control stations were hit in Staromlynivka and Pokrovsk in Donetsk Oblast and Pokrovske in Zaporizhzhia Oblast.
In addition, a Russian ammunition depot was struck in Dovzhansk, Luhansk Oblast. Fuel and lubricant storage facilities used by Russian forces were hit in Rovenky, Luhansk Oblast, and Berdiansk, Zaporizhzhia Oblast.
Ukrainian forces struck sites in Suvorove and Rysove in temporarily occupied Crimea equipped with Russian automated surveillance systems known as Grenader, used to monitor and detect movement.

articles.title: Russia threatens Europe with a “very short war” if Western troops are deployed in Ukraine — CCD
articles.body:
Russia threatens Europe with a “very short war” if Western troops are deployed in Ukraine — CCD
Ukrinform reports this, citing the Center for Countering Disinformation (CCD) at the National Security and Defense Council of Ukraine, in a Telegram post.
“Russia has once again intensified its aggressive rhetoric toward Ukraine’s European partners, resorting to ultimatums and blatant threats of military confrontation. Russian Foreign Minister Sergei Lavrov said that the possible deployment of Western forces in Ukraine would constitute a ‘declaration of war’ against Russia. He also threatened Europe with a ‘very short war’ if ‘Europe attacks Russia,’” the statement said.
According to the CCD, the Kremlin chose the “International Youth Festival” in Yekaterinburg, which brought together many foreign guests, as the venue for another round of threats and intimidation.
In his speech, Lavrov employed a classic mirror-propaganda tactic: against the backdrop of Russia’s ongoing war of aggression against Ukraine and its constant provocations against European states, he began talking about the “threat of an attack by Europe.”
Through such manipulation, Moscow is attempting to shift responsibility for the escalation onto Western governments and justify its own aggressive actions. The propaganda is aimed both at Russia’s domestic audience and at foreigners. The Kremlin’s aggressive rhetoric once again demonstrates that Russia is not seeking ways to achieve peace but is using every public platform to blackmail the international community, the CCD said.
As previously reported by Ukrinform, Ukrainian Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha responded to another propaganda statement by Russian Foreign Minister Sergei Lavrov about the alleged need to eradicate “Nazism in Europe.” In particular, he stressed that achieving this goal would require a special military operation in the European part of Russia.

articles.title: The Guardian view on the Houthi advance in Yemen: another vital Middle East artery becomes a battlefield | Editorial
articles.body:
Even in a region beset by turmoil and learning to expect the unexpected, the lightning advance of Yemen’s Houthis along the Red Sea coast has shocked observers. More than 100,000 people have been forced to flee in a country where immiseration and displacement have become routine and half the population depend on humanitarian aid. But outsiders are paying close attention, because by claiming thousands of kilometres in a matter of days, and seizing strategically important islands, the Iran-backed rebels now control the Bab al-Mandab strait – the other major regional energy chokepoint after the Hormuz strait.
The Iran war has forced Saudi Arabia to rely on moving oil via its east-west pipeline to Red Sea ports. Now drone strikes – blamed on an Iran-backed militia in Iraq – have shut the pipeline: on one estimate, a month-long closure could cut global crude supply by 120m barrels. The halt to shipping through the Bab al-Mandab strait could be much more protracted. Taking the oil north is a far slower and more expensive route to Asian markets, and does not preclude attacks by the Houthis, who are also targeting oil facilities.
Saudi Arabia had painfully extracted itself from a war with the Houthis which it recklessly spearheaded – nominally in support of the internationally recognised government – at astounding cost to its own coffers and Yemeni civilians. It apparently hoped that it could calibrate its response to a flight from Iran to Houthi-controlled Sana’a in July, the first in over a decade, sufficiently to save the 2022 truce. But bombing Sana’a airport gave the Houthis the opportunity to escalate while blaming Riyadh.
The Houthis are not mere proxies for Tehran, but their interests are increasingly aligned, thanks to Donald Trump’s unlawful war on Iran. They need to maintain Iranian support and the strait of Hormuz crisis has created a new opportunity to exert economic pressure, and perhaps create a new income stream, via strategic gains along the coast. The forces ranged against them, including the government and southern secessionists, are more fractured than ever. The United Arab Emirates, which has clashed with its former close partner Saudi Arabia, withdrew its troops at the turn of the year.
Saudi strikes alone will not be enough to push the Houthis back. But Mr Trump has rebuffed requests for help. The Houthis have been canny enough to say that they are targeting only the Saudis, though that message reinforces the fact that their leverage could be used more broadly in future. They are also closer than ever to Djibouti, home to US, Chinese and other military bases.
The Saudis face a choice between negotiations with an emboldened enemy now making increasingly maximalist demands – or returning to the kind of full-scale war they previously regretted, with little support this time. Turkey and Pakistan are not rushing to act on the new Mecca defence pact the three countries signed in August.
Yemen’s recent history amply demonstrates the futility of seeking a military solution. Ultimately, its citizens deserve a government not dependent on either Riyadh or Tehran. Outside parties should concentrate on promoting a political process within the country. They should stress that both sides must protect civilians, and support humanitarian efforts. Their priority, however, should be a resolution to the Iran war, without which danger in the region, and broader instability, will only grow.

articles.title: Over half of eligible Iranians join Jan Fada campaign
articles.body:
Over half of eligible Iranians join Jan Fada campaign
TEHRAN – The “Jan Fada” (self-sacrificing volunteer) campaign officially launched on March 29 as a spontaneous public movement in response to persistent threats and aggression by the United States and Israel against Iran’s territorial integrity and sovereignty.
More than half of the country’s eligible citizens have registered for the initiative, according to Jan Fada spokesperson Sasan Zare, making it one of the largest public mobilization drives in the country in recent years.
Speaking at a press conference in Tehran on Wednesday, Zare said more than 31.3 million people had registered so far. He described the campaign as an initiative aimed at demonstrating public readiness to defend the country and contribute to various national sectors.
“Of the 31 million people who took part in the campaign, 32 percent were women and 68 percent were men. Notably, the participants were predominantly young, with more than 60 percent under the age of 46,” he said.
According to Zare, 26 percent of volunteers expressed an interest in military and security activities, while 20 percent opted for relief and rescue operations and assistance to those affected. Another 20 percent selected social services, 17 percent volunteered for cultural, artistic, and media activities, and 13 percent offered to provide ongoing financial support. The remaining five percent were classified under miscellaneous services.
Organizers have described Jan Fada as a contemporary expression of Iran’s longstanding tradition of national resilience. The initiative, launched to demonstrate public readiness to defend the country amid heightened geopolitical tensions, quickly attracted millions of registrants nationwide.
The campaign has since expanded from a public registration drive into a broader framework for organized civic participation and national solidarity, bringing together volunteers from diverse communities.
The Jan Fada headquarters has also announced the launch of training and organizational preparations for 1,000 national resistance battalions.
The announcement follows strong public interest and repeated appeals from citizens seeking to stand alongside the country’s armed forces in defending the nation.
According to the organizers, close coordination with military authorities has paved the way for translating the campaign’s broad public participation into structured tactical units.
